News.title: Counter-terror police reopen attempted burglary probe as part of Widdecombe inquiry
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the death of ex-MP Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into a report of an attempted burglary at a London address in April last year.

No arrests were made at the time and the investigation was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.

On Friday Counter Terrorism Policing said a line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

Counter Terrorism Policing London has made a mandatory referral over its handling of the initial investigation to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).

The Metropolitan Police had received a report of an attempted burglary in the Greater London area, the statement said, with the initial investigation carried out by the Metropolitan Police and Counter Terrorism Policing London.

The police watchdog has said it is investigating allegations that a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member "failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry" related to the attempted burglary.

The 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse claims at Army college
News.content:
AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.

North Yorkshire Police told the BBC in a response to a Freedom of Information Act request it had received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, including allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault.

No information was included on whether the reports had led to prosecutions.

A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.

The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.

One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room.

"They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to.

"And then I was rapedâ¦ by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."

Streeting said he sympathised with the women who had been "badly failed", and praised them for speaking up.

"We have a duty to uphold the very highest standards in uniform and to treat every woman with the dignity and respect she deserves.

"I don't want anyone who has the ambition and talent to join our armed forces to be deterred, so it's contingent on us to make sure that we've got our act together," he added.

Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training.

Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".

Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.

She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."

The MoD told the BBC that the college "welcomes external scrutiny and challenge".

It said that AFC had in the last year "hosted the safeguarding bodies, parliamentarians, the Children's Commissioner's office and the Armed Forces Commissioner, as well as receiving an outstanding report from Ofsted".

Earlier this week, Sarah Atherton, former MP for Wrexham, told the BBC that public confidence in the college could "only be restored through an independent inquiry".

Atherton, who previously served in the Army's Intelligence Corps, led a 2021 government review into the experiences of women in the armed forces.

Emma Lewell MP said: "If this was any other school or residential environment for children, it would have been closed down."

The Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza said she would ensure the "appalling attacks" were investigated and "those responsible, including for failing to safeguard these girls, are held to account".

She said all children living away from home had a right to contact her team for support, and that she would make sure all girls at AFC could do so.

News.title: Watch: BBC asks Infantino if he will resign as Fifa president
News.content:
The BBC has asked Fifa president Gianni Infantino if he has the support of football's South American governing body, Conmebol.

The Fifa head has faced multiple calls to resign after his highly controversial attempt to sell private stakes in the World Cup, which he later abandoned.

Infantino, who did not answer the BBC's questions, was in Colombia for the inauguration of the country's new President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The BBC's South America correspondent Ione Wells later asked the Fifa president if he would step down.

News.title: Obesity rates have doubled in England since 1993 - what's going on?
News.content:
If England's obesity rates were still the same as 1993 there would be seven million fewer adults living with obesity.

There are 14 million adults classified as obese, despite successive governments launching 14 separate obesity strategies over the past three decades.

It's clear something isn't working, so what's behind the increase?

And can anything be done about it?

According to new analysis by the King's Fund, 15% of England's adult population - those aged 16 and over - in 1993 was obese, with rates achieving a record high of 30% in 2024.

Their analysis suggests obesity rates are rising fastest in 16-to-24 year-olds, with 18% classified as obese or severely obese in 2024 compared with just 6% in 1993.

Accounting for population change, this means there are now one million young adults living with obesity in England - 700,000 more than if rates had not risen over the past three decades.

Dave Buck, senior fellow for public health at the King's Fund, called this rise "clearly worrying" and says governments have "talked the talk, but not sufficiently walked the walk" in addressing obesity rates.

"This analysis shows the scale of the failure to take the necessary action on tackling this obesity timebomb," he added.

News.title: Thai PM vows to introduce stricter gun laws after eight killed in shooting
News.content:
Police Colonel Thadsakorn Konthong said that the gun and bullets used in the attack belonged to the teen's grandfather, with an initial inspection finding signs that the firearm had been searched for inside the grandfather's bedroom.

International and local media have reported that the gun was legally registered and had a permit.

Thailand has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in South East Asia, with around 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, around four million of which are believed to be owned illegally.

The country has strict gun laws, which punish the illegal possession of arms with up to 10 years in jail, but enforcement of these laws has been an issue.

During his time as interior minister, Anutin introduced a number of gun control laws, including a short-term ban on new gun licenses and import restrictions.

Speaking on Friday, the prime minister said the tragedy "shouldn't have happened".

"I don't just feel sorry for the victims but I feel sorry that this happened. How can this happen in our country," Anutin added.

News.title: US appeals court halts Trump ballroom project paving way for Supreme Court showdown
News.content:
President Trump has asserted that the new ballroom is needed to "accommodate people for grand parties, State Visits", and has also said that it is "vital for National Security".

The ballroom building would consist of the large entertaining space above ground and also a security complex below ground. Trump doubled down on the need for the space after an assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner in April.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation celebrated the ruling on Friday, noting that no above-ground construction can take place "unless and until" Congress takes action.

"The White House, a global landmark that symbolizes American identity and the ideals of democracy, belongs to the American people," said Brent Leggs, President and CEO of the National Trust.

"The National Trust for Historic Preservation and its partners are proud to defend this irreplaceable monument on behalf of all Americans."

Trump has touted the ballroom project repeatedly since he unveiled plans for it in July 2025. It would have been the most substantial structural change to the presidential residence in more than 70 years.

But the project has been mired in legal issues since October, when the Trump administration demolished the East Wing, which was built in 1902, to begin construction. Trump initially said the project would be "near" the East Wing, not that it would be demolished.

Government lawyers have argued the additional security complex and features included in the ballroom project are needed to protect the White House complex from drones, ballistic missiles, biohazards and other threats - changes essential to protecting the president, his family, and staff. Trump said on Friday that construction includes bomb shelters, hospital and medical facilities and top secret military facilities.

But the Trust said there was no basis to "disturb" the White House and argued that having a ballroom isn't a national security emergency.

The three-judge appeals court panel said on Friday that its ruling "has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable", nor does it weigh in on whether the administration may ultimately construct the ballroom.

"What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court's expeditious litigation without securing Congress's authorization, as the Constitution and laws require," the order said.

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Streeting said the government is taking the issue "extremely seriously".

"We should never have been put in a position where prisons across the country were so full-to-bursting that any government, let alone this government, had to contemplate the early release of people from serious convictions that have led to being in prison in the first place.

"We're not pretending this is okay."

He pointed to "strong controls" and supervision that will be in place for people released into the community and added that the government is "determined" to build more prison places and is looking carefully into the exemptions under the scheme.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Blaik said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.

If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation
News.content:
The University of Cambridge will review its process for appointing senior academics following the resignation of Jason Arday in the midst of a plagiarism row.

The institution said findings from an investigation into the education professor's academic qualifications and appointments would "feed into" a new review on the appointment process for senior academic roles.

The Jesus College fellow has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work, with attention now turning to Cambridge's handling of concerns and his upcoming memoir.

News of the review comes after a group of academics called for an independent probe into his appointment.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Cambridge said on Friday that it was "fully aware of the public commentary and concerns" and would "continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday's appointment and tenure". A spokesperson declined to comment further.

It previously announced an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments on Wednesday, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

Jesus College welcomed the appointments review, saying Arday's role as fellow there had been "contingent on his university position".

"We rely on the university to do checks on academic credentials for its appointments," a spokeswoman added.

The University of Glasgow, where Arday worked for just over a year before moving to Cambridge, has commissioned its own review of his appointment.

"Jason Arday was employed as Professor of Sociology of Education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023," a statement said.

"The Principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future."

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

It told the BBC on Friday that its position remains unchanged in light of recent events and that his PhD "still stands".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic positions have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus", which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

News.title: Madonna and Blur producer William Orbit dies aged 69
News.content:
Acclaimed British music producer William Orbit, known for his work with acts including Madonna, Blur, All Saints and Pink, has died at the age of 69.

A statement, external released on Friday by Orbit's family and friends "with profound sadness" said he died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given.

"He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness," the statement said.

London-born Orbit, who real name was William Wainwright, helped to reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with the album Ray of Light, which blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop.

It went on to win three Grammy Awards and remains, for many people, the Queen of Pop's greatest record.

News.title: Police make further arrests as Thetford disorder continues
News.content:
More arrests have been made over disorder linked to anti-immigration protests that saw crowds attempt to storm the homes of suspected asylum seekers and a police officer "seriously bitten".

Asylum seekers were removed from properties in Thetford on Thursday for their own safety, Norfolk Police said.

Two men in their 40s were arrested as protests in the market town continued for a third night, and a woman was arrested on Friday in relation to an assault on a police officer, bringing the total number detained to six.

Protesters attempted to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living on Tuesday and Wednesday night, when officers were also "subjected to significant aggression".

News.title: Brothers jailed for killing man and injuring his son while racing cars home
News.content:
Following sentencing, Rhys' wife Caroline Jenkins, also known as Carrie, said in a statement she often wondered what difference it would have made to her family's future "if we'd hugged a little tighter and a little longer" when she waved them off that day.

She said, for her son, life "without a dad who was involved in everything you did is a hard adjustment" and it "carried an element of PTSD".

Carrie said Ioan was emotionally and physically scarred by the crash.

"It's impossible to convey the full impact Rhys' death had on us," she said, and there remains a "massive hole left in our lives by his unnecessary death".

Ioan, who broke both arms, and suffered a fractured rib and perforated bowel, said he wished his dad was still here to "watch me grow up and be my dad".

Rhys' youngest son, Gruff, was six when the crash happened.

In his own victim impact statement, he said he was in bed when police arrived to tell his mum what had happened.

After being told his dad had died, he said: "I ran out of the house. I didn't know where I was going. It was the worst feeling of my life."

The court was told Umar Ben Yusaf's car was not directly involved in the crash, but the "competitive" nature of his driving with Abubakr Ben Yusaf contributed significantly.

Judge Timothy Petts said the trauma the Jenkins family had been through in the last 21 months was "difficult for me to summarise".

"You have all been suffering with your own devastating grief but also trying to deal with the practical consequences of Rhys's death and Ioan's injuries.

"It has been an horrendous time for all of you," he told them.

Petts said to Umar and Abubakr Ben Yusaf that he was satisfied they were racing each other.

"Both of you were constantly riding your luck at high speed, completely unnecessarily, and eventually it ran out with appalling consequences.

"Rhys Jenkins never stood a chance because you were so close to him when you lost control. He was driving perfectly properly and did nothing wrong. He had no time to avoid the collision."

Sgt Sara John, from Dyfed-Powys Police's serious collision investigation unit, said: "The sentences passed today cannot undo the tragic loss suffered by Rhys's family."

She added she hoped the outcome "provides them with some closure as they begin to move forward with their lives, which have been changed forever".

"The actions of Abubakr and Umar Yusaf on that day were catastrophic. Their choice to drive in the manner they did shows their utter disregard towards other road users."

News.title: Girl, 11, found dead after search at Midlothian beauty spot
News.content:
An 11-year-old girl has died after being found in the water at a beauty spot in Midlothian.

A major search was launched over reports of concern for the girl in Gore Glen Woodland Park, near Gorebridge, at about 12:40 on Thursday.

The girl's body was found in the park's Gore Water, near Shank Bridge, at about 16:25. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Her death is being treated as unexplained and inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances."

The force said the girl's family was aware.

News.title: England footballer Toney charged with assault in Soho
News.content:
England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.

The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged on 31 July following an incident on Wardour Street in Soho on 6 December.

The former Brentford striker, who started England's 6-4 win over France in the "bronze final" of the World Cup last month, has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 24 September.

A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."

After starting his career at Northampton Town, the striker had permanent spells at Newcastle, Peterborough and Brentford before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2024.

He was a surprise selection for England's World Cup squad but apart from the France game, his only other appearance was as a late substitute in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina.

News.title: Two firms guilty over man killed by falling window
News.content:
Two companies have been found guilty of health and safety breaches after a coach driver was killed by a falling window pane.

Mick Ferris, 53, died when glass weighing 130kg fell 300ft (90m) from a penthouse flat at The Corniche tower block on Albert Embankment in central London in October 2018.

St James Group Ltd and specialist contractors Lindner Prater Ltd were convicted at Inner London Crown Court of "failing to discharge a duty" under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. The firms will be sentenced on 24 September.

Foster + Partners, the architecture firm behind The Gherkin, and engineering consultants Wintech Ltd were cleared of the same charges.

During the trial, the court heard the "extraordinary" fact that a window panel had already fallen from the same development in August 2017, and the design was not substantially changed as a result.

Prosecuting, Gordon Menzies said: "It's reasonably practicable for clever people to do a simple thing and design a window that doesn't fall out once every year."

Andy Burnham has said it "insane" that the UK has hosted only one World Cup, accusing Fifa and Uefa of conspiring against the home nations.

The Prime Minister questioned if the organisations had "something against us", with the UK not hosting the World Cup since 1966.

Mr Burnham referenced his involvement in England's doomed 2010 bid for the 2018 World Cup, which was awarded to Russia.

The controversy around that process, and the 2022 Qatar World Cup, eventually unseated then-Fifa president Sepp Blatter and other senior officials.

England’s bid only received two votes from 22 members of the Fifa executive committee, amid claims of bribery.

Andy Burnham, pictured during a football match between Labour Party members and journalists in 2016, is an Everton fan ( Danny Lawson/PA )

Mr Blatter’s replacement, Gianni Infantino, is currently under fire for proposals to sell shares in the World Cup to private investors.

Mr Burnham, an Everton fan, was speaking to the Away Days podcast, which showed him looking through classic Everton, England and Liverpool shirts.

He had been culture, media and sports secretary in the run-up to the World Cup bid being submitted, when he was part of Gordon Brown’s cabinet.

The podcast’s host, Ellis Platten, said to the Prime Minister: “The fact we’ve only ever hosted one World Cup in Britain is insane to me.”

Mr Burnham replied: “Definitely. I don’t know, it makes you wonder whether the authorities at the European and global level have something against us, I don’t know.

“The country that invented the game, you know, you’d think we would have had a bit more of that attention. I have been part of Governments that have tried to bring the World Cup here, it’s just the voting.

“Let’s be honest, some of the practices within football haven’t supported even-handed decision-making. I’m being diplomatic here, but it’s not good, is it?”

Despite not hosting the World Cup for 60 years, the UK has hosted games at the men’s European Championships twice and fixtures at the 2028 tournament will be played in the UK and Ireland.

Meanwhile, the UK will host the women’s World Cup in 2035. It hosted the 2005 and 2022 women’s European Championships. The latter saw England’s women win the tournament for the first time on home soil.

Since entering Downing Street himself, Mr Burnham has called for Mr Infantino to resign, saying he is the “wrong man” to lead Fifa over his bungled attempt to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

He told journalists: “I do not believe that he is the right man to lead football forward on the world stage.

“The plan that was put forward was offensive to many people, football people, around the world, and it can’t be the case that we just move on and forget that, it wasn’t acceptable.”

News.title: Counter-terror police investigating Ann Widdecombe death reopen attempted burglary probe
News.content:

Counter-terror police investigating the death of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an old probe into an attempted burglary in London last year.

The incident at an address in Greater London was reported in April 2025.

No arrests were made after an investigation by the Metropolitan Police and Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP), and the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.

Since it was reopened, CTP London has identified a line of inquiry “which may have been relevant” but was “not identified and pursued by them at the time”.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is now investigating the “conduct” of a CTP London staff member, following an allegation that the employee “failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry” related to the attempted burglary.

Reform UK spokeswoman and former Tory minister Ms Widdecombe, 78, died on 8 July after she was hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon.

Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged with her murder on 20 July.

open image in gallery Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her property in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, last month ( PA )

Senior national co-ordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.”

She added: “Given the nature of this matter and the significant public interest in the investigation into Ann Widdecombe’s death, it was of critical importance for us to provide this update.”

CTP London made a “mandatory conduct referral” to the IOPC on Friday.

An IOPC spokesperson said: “We can confirm that the IOPC has decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier today.

“The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025.

“Counter Terrorism Policing London has been notified of our decision, and no further information is available at this early stage.”

Some would-be immigrants from the Dominican Republic now have to post bonds of up to $250,000 each under a Trump administration initiative to keep them from collecting government benefits in the U.S., according to reports.

The Department of State's pilot program covers Dominicans who've previously been denied visas on grounds they could become what's known as a “public charge,” The Washington Free Beacon was first to report.

A public charge is someone who's “primarily dependent on the government for subsistence,” either by “receiving public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization at government expense,” according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

The pilot program, which began Wednesday, will reportedly require potential public charges from the Dominican Republic to post bonds of $100,000 to $250,000 that would be forfeited if they use American government benefits, such as food stamps, housing vouchers or Medicaid.

“We are piloting public charge bonds in the Dominican Republic based on the scope and scale of our immigrant visa operations at the U.S. Embassy in Santo Domingo,” a State Department spokesperson said in a Friday statement to The Independent. “Consular officers will set bond amounts based on an assessment of the totality of the circumstances of each case.”

open image in gallery The Department of State is requiring some would-be immigrants from the Dominican Republic to post bonds of up to $250,000 each so they don’t collect government benefits in the US ( Reuters )

The program may be expanded to cover immigrants from other countries, the Free Beacon said.

State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Bloomberg Law, “Immigrating to the United States is a privilege, not a right.”

“Those who seek to obtain that privilege must be capable of demonstrating that they will be a benefit —rather than a burden — to our nation,” he added.

The visa bonds are the costliest measure imposed on immigrants and other visitors to the U.S. by President Donald Trump's administration, according to Bloomberg Law.

Trump's 2024 campaign included pledges to restrict immigration and carry out the largest mass deportation operation in U.S. history.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump campaigned for office on pledges to restrict immigration and carry out the largest mass deportation operation in US history ( Getty )

The new visa bonds will be refundable after five years if visa holders haven’t needed any government assistance, the Free Beacon said.

USCIS can also reportedly decide when to cancel a bond or declare it's been breached and subject to forfeiture.

Last year, the State Department began a one-year pilot program that required tourists and business travelers from 50 countries, including 30 in Africa, to post visa bonds of $5,000 to $15,500, according to PBS.

The program was made permanent in a rule published Monday in the Federal Register.

It also increased the amount of the bonds to $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000, to be set by American consular officials.

The Center for Immigration Studies, which favors lower immigration to the U.S., said in a February study that 53 percent of immigrant households “used one or more major welfare programs” in 2024, compared to 37 percent of U.S.-born households.

A January study by the libertarian Cato Institute think tank, however, found that in 2023, immigrants to the U.S. comprised 14.8 percent of the population and received just 10.4 percent of “means-tested welfare and entitlement benefits” on a per capita basis.

A two-year-old girl, whose parents successfully sued a Texas hospital to prevent brain-death testing after she drowned in a hotel pool, has died after being removed from life support.

Annelise Camp’s family confirmed her passing this week, weeks after a judge granted a temporary injunction in their favor.

Her parents, Johnston and Joy Camp, released a statement saying Annelise "is now with Jesus." They added, "While our hearts are broken, we trust in His perfect love, His faithfulness, and His promises."

Annelise was found unconscious in a hotel pool on Memorial Day and subsequently admitted to Texas Children's Hospital in Houston.

Days later, her parents petitioned a judge to block doctors from conducting brain-death tests, asserting she still showed signs of life and deserved more time to recover and explore treatment options.

Court documents, as reported by The Texas Tribune, indicated Annelise’s heart was beating, though she relied on a ventilator.

The Camps also sought to transfer her to another facility for alternative treatments.

Texas Children’s, however, maintained its desire to perform testing to guide her medical care, stating it had no immediate plans to cease treatment.

( AP )

Hospital officials noted they had contacted 36 medical facilities regarding a transfer, with 35 declining and the remaining one requiring brain-death testing before consideration.

The family eventually secured a transfer for Annelise to a hospital in Louisiana.

State legislator Rep. Steve Toth informed The New York Times that Annelise was later brought back to Texas about a week ago, receiving care at Christus Mother Frances Hospital in Tyler.

Annelise’s grandfather, Steve Camp, posted online that her breathing tubes were removed on Monday, and "When this procedure was done, she passed very quickly."

The family has not publicly stated the reasons behind the decision to remove her from life support.

The family’s legal battle garnered support from organizations like Texas Right to Life, which stated online, "This victory gave the Camp family two extra months with Annelise and provided her a chance to recover from her injury."

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton also weighed in, posting on X in June, "Annelise Camp is fighting for her life and deserves a medical team that will fight just as hard."

Texas law defines brain death as the irreversible cessation of brain function, allowing hospitals to withdraw life-sustaining measures once a patient is declared brain-dead.

Johnston Camp told KRIV-TV in June, "The big common denominator is time. And so when you have time, I know scientifically you can see a certain reading, but she is showing progressive results from her body or complexions, her vitals."

In July, the Camps had shared on a GoFundMe page that Annelise continued to show "encouraging signs" at the Louisiana hospital, adding, "We are pursuing every available option, including specialized and exploratory treatments that show promise."

A church service for Annelise is scheduled for next Wednesday in Houston.

When CBS News' Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss's hand-picked star anchor Tony Dokoupil took a two week vacation, a curious thing happened; more people actually watched his show.

During his two-week hiatus, another CBS journalist — Matt Gutman — filled in behind the CBS Evening News desk. During his first week, Gutman drew 4.1 million viewers, which was the program's best performance in 17 weeks and the first time it exceeded 4 million viewers since the end of March, according to media journalist Oliver Darcy of Status.

Whether or not the audience is rejecting Dokoupil, embracing Gutman, or a little bit of both, remains to be seen.

Dokoupil was one of Weiss's earliest staffing announcements after she took over the network in October. He pulled 4 million viewers during the week of June 22, but he hadn't attracted more than that since late March, according to Status.

CBS's evening news show has struggled to consistently hit 4 million mark since Weiss took over.

Tony Dokoupil, host of the CBS Evening News, went on vacation for two weeks in late July and during his absence the show’s ratings exceeded 4 million viewers for the first time since late March ( Getty )

With the station already struggling through its transition — and many of those struggles have been quite public — critics questioned Dokoupil’s decision to take two weeks off this early into his hosting tenure.

"Summer is when the second and third place networks try to make progress against the first place anchor who goes on vacation. In this case, the third place anchor took off for two weeks — a baffling move given his collapsing show — and his substitute outclassed him in the ratings," Darcy quoted an unnamed TV executive as saying.

The same source described the outperformance by the host's substitute as "another dagger in Tony's neck."

A CBS spokesperson told The Independent that Dokoupil has the network’s support and said the reporting around his performance has been misleading.

CBS pointed out that all network newscasts – CBS Evening News, ABC World News Tonight and NBC Nightly News – had more viewers in the week of July 27 than July 20.

A spokesperson for the network told The Independent: "The week of 7/27 just generated more news, which is why all numbers were up for every show. Claiming it has something to do with a Matt/Tony split is false.”

They also said that Dokoupil had been "consistently trending up" and that the "network has confidence in Tony," with a ratings growth in Q2, the first for the show since 2020, as well as 4.1 million viewers for the individual broadcast on July 21.

After Weiss named Dokoupil as the new anchor at CBS Evening News, Vanity Fair published an article questioning "more than 20 current and former CBS staffers and industry insiders" about the reporter's reputation at the network.

One of the respondents described Dokoupil as a "useful idiot" for Weiss, and another suggested he was "deeply lacking in self-awareness."

The CBS spokesperson pointed to a more recent feature about Dokoupil in Variety focusing on the anchor’s innovative storytelling as further evidence of his success.

During his run as host, the show's programming has been notably more friendly to President Donald Trump and his administration. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has appeared numerous times on his show, while Dokoupil agreed to do an "embedded" interview with former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem while she was in charge of ICE. His show also ran a segment offering a "salute" to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, describing him as the "ultimate Florida Man."

Weiss, the founder of the “anti-woke” media outlet The Free Press, was controversially appointed editor-in-chief of CBS News in October 2025, despite having no previous broadcast experience.

Dokoupil returns to the CBS Evening News desk on Monday.

The Independent has requested comment from CBS.

CNN’s Sara Sidner said she faced a terrifying health scare after a recent PET scan came back with potentially concerning results.

The network’s longtime news anchor, 54, was diagnosed with stage 3 breast cancer in 2023. She shared the diagnosis on-air with viewers in January 2024, revealing that she was in her second month of chemotherapy. She was declared cancer-free later that year.

During Friday morning’s segment of the CNN News Central program, Sidner, 54, recalled the recent follow-up appointment.

She said the PET scan came back “lit up like a Christmas tree.” “It indicated I was likely metastatic, stage 4 cancer, incurable. It appeared to have spread to my hip, my spine, my liver, my lungs. I was inconsolable at the time,” she remembered. “I thought cancer had spread all over my body.”

Sidner immediately began thinking the worst. “I looked up, ‘How long do I have to live?’” she asked the doctor. “The number came back, less than five years. It knocked the breath out of me, as you might imagine. Then I cried.”

open image in gallery Sara Sidner was diagnosed with stage 3 breast cancer in November 2023 ( Getty )

open image in gallery Sidner was declared cancer-free in 2024 ( Getty )

To double-check the findings, the doctors performed a biopsy. The results took just over two weeks to come back, which Sidner described as “fifteen days of torture.”

The biopsy came back malignant. To confirm the results, she took a molecular cancer blood test. “Not cancer. Again, shock because this scan suggested otherwise,” she added. “The doctor then made very clear, biopsy beats scan. I had a deep, guttural sigh of relief.”

She remembered a “lump of tears” gathering in her throat when she heard the news.

Sidner has worked for CNN for 18 years, joining the network in 2008 as a national and international correspondent. In 2022, she launched and hosted her own show, Big Picture with Sara Sidner, which aired on the company’s short-lived CNN+ streaming service. The following year, she officially transitioned to co-host CNN News Central.

She has continued to use her platform to emphasize the importance of annual breast cancer screenings, as well as conducting regular self-examinations.

“I have thanked cancer for choosing me,” Sidner said on-air in 2024. “I am learning that no matter what hell we go through in life that I am still madly in love with this life. And just being alive feels really different for me now. I am happier because I don’t stress about foolish little things that used to annoy me. And now every single day that I breathe another breath, I can celebrate that I am still here with you, I am still here with my co-anchors, my colleagues, my family, and I can love and cry and laugh and hope. And that my dear friends, is enough.”

News.title: Lindsay Clancy’s doctor details her five-day psychiatric hospital stay before children’s killings
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Lindsay Clancy's doctor took the stand Friday and detailed her behavior during a nearly five-day psychiatric hospital stay a few weeks before she killed her three children.

The Massachusetts mother’s hospital visit is a key chapter in both the prosecution and defense narratives about her mental state when she strangled the children in their suburban home and then jumped out a second-story window.

In questioning one of her McLean Hospital psychiatrists on Friday, a prosecutor underscored that Clancy denied to hospital clinicians that she wanted to hurt anyone else or planned to kill herself.

Clancy's lawyer, meanwhile, aimed to flesh out the defense's claim that she sought mental health help for months, wasn't properly diagnosed as she went from provider to provider, and was put on a series of medications that left her worse off.

open image in gallery The defense doesn't dispute that she killed the children but says she shouldn't be held criminally responsible, contending that she was so mentally ill that she heard voices telling her to kill them and herself ( AP Photo/Rodrique Ngowi )

Clancy has pleaded not guilty to murder charges in the January 2023 strangling deaths of Callan, Dawson and Cora Clancy, who ranged from 8 months to 5 years old. They were found in the basement of the family's home in coastal Duxbury, Massachusetts, and their mother was lying, badly injured, in the yard. She remains paralyzed from the waist down.

Prosecutors argue that Clancy, a 35-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, was an intentional killer who attacked her children after getting her husband out of the house by asking him to run errands. The defense doesn't dispute that she killed the children but says she shouldn't be held criminally responsible, contending that she was so mentally ill that she heard voices telling her to kill them and herself.

In the criminal trial and a medical malpractice lawsuit, Clancy's attorneys say she had bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis — a break with reality that a small fraction of women have after childbirth — that weren't fully diagnosed until after the killings, though one of her outpatient providers considered bipolar disorder in 2022.

Clancy recounted that provider's opinion and disagreed with it after she checked herself into McLean early on New Year's Day 2023, psychiatrist Dr. Alia Goodheart told jurors Friday.

When Goodheart joined Clancy's lineup of providers that Jan. 3, the patient expressed concerns about an antipsychotic medication she'd previously been prescribed to help with insomnia, and about feeling numb, which can be a side effect of that drug, Goodheart said. She diagnosed her with insomnia with a mental health condition and tapered down the medication.

Clancy then reported she could sleep, was eager to go home in time for a long-planned belated birthday party for Cora, and booked herself follow-up outpatient care, the psychiatrist testified. The hospital discharged her that Jan. 5 with prescriptions for an antianxiety drug and a sleep aid.

open image in gallery Clancy’s handwritten notes detailing her mental health struggles were shown at trial ( Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledge )

“She had never stated that she had any thoughts of harming anybody else,” Goodheart told jurors. And although Clancy said she'd had suicidal thoughts, she denied having them in the moment and indeed said she had reasons not to take her own life: “her children and her family, her mother,” Goodheart recalled.

When defense lawyer Kevin Reddington had his turn to question the psychiatrist, he emphasized that the hospital care team didn't do various tests — Goodheart said they weren't necessary — or learn that she had called a suicide hotline that fall. Nor did the providers talk to various outpatient clinicians who had treated Clancy over the prior months, though they did speak to her husband.

“She was very sick, wasn’t she?” Reddington asked at one point.

“I don’t know what you mean,” Goodheart responded.

If convicted of murder, Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week. If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you

News.title: Gomes scores for Aston Villa in defeat by Bayern Munich in Hong Kong
News.content:
Aston Villa 1 Bayern Munich 2

Aston Villa’s tour of the Far East ended in defeat as they lost 2-1 to German champions Bayern Munich in a pre-season friendly at the Kai Tak Sports Park in Hong Kong on Friday.

Bayern took the lead inside the final 10 minutes of the first half, with defender Kim Min-jae heading in from Tom Bischof’s sublime free-kick. Villa goalkeeper Marco Bizot made a string of saves in the second half to keep Bayern’s lead at one goal until former Liverpool forward Luis Díaz smashed in Bayern’s second off the underside of the bar.

Just as the game appeared to be out of reach for Aston Villa, who had struggled to create much going forward for most of the game, Unai Emery’s side showed some life late on. Summer signing João Gomes’s goal from the edge of the box gave them hope before Tammy Abraham nearly brought them back onto level terms, only to be denied by a fine save from 40-year-old Manuel Neuer.

Aston Villa are next in action in six days’ time when they take on Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup before kicking off their Premier League campaign at Brighton. Bayern have one more friendly to come against RB Leipzig before the DFL-Supercup against Borussia Dortmund. They then kick off the defence of their Bundesliga crown against Stuttgart at home on August 28.

News.title: Suspected Ebola case on packed Congo river boat sparks testing rush
News.content:
Congolese health authorities have intercepted and detained a river boat on its way to the capital after a suspected Ebola case onboard.

Authorities have set up a mobile clinic to test more than 200 passengers after one of them disembarked and died earlier on the voyage.

The boat travelling from the northeastern commercial hub of Kisangani was stopped and held in Maluku, some 40 miles from Kinshasa.

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is dealing with its worst ever outbreak of the viral haemorrhagic fever, which has seen nearly 4,000 cases and killed around 1,801 people according to the latest government figures.

Samuel Roger Kamba, the health minister, said a 32-year-old man had disembarked in Pimu in Mongala province, before developing ‌suspected Ebola symptoms and dying.

“We did not say it was Ebola. We said there was a suspected case for which we are being cautious,” the health minister told a press conference, according to MediaCongo, a local news site.

He said there had been no other reports of deaths among travellers.

The virus has so far spread to five provinces, though more than 90 per cent of cases have been recorded in the north eastern Ituri region.

News.title: The best luxury hotels in the Cotswolds
News.content:
From gracious old farmsteads and magnificent manor houses to an ancient coaching inn creaking with Tudor character, the top luxury hotels in the Cotswolds combine a wonderful sense of history with contemporary style and outstanding modern British cuisine. Whether near picturesque Broadway in the north of the region or close to Bath in the south, location is a key attribute to them all: some offer serene escapes in acres of their own rolling parkland; others sit amid superb gardens; and several take over classic honey-stone villages that look as if they have been beamed in from a halcyon era of the past.

They all excel in providing creature comforts, whether crackling fires by kick-back sofas, canopy beds with soft throws, or suites with terraces and hot tubs. Facilities are top-notch too, ranging from beautiful bars and quiet terraces to blissful spas with inviting pools and even an opportunity for equine adventures. News.title: El Nino could cause explosion of rabid seals, animal health experts warn
News.content:
This year’s El Nino weather event risks propelling an outbreak of rabid seals around the world, the world’s animal health body has warned.

Countries in South America and Australasia are being urged to look for signs the deadly infectious disease has reached their waters, only two years after it was first confirmed in South Africa.

The 2024 discovery of rabies in South Africa’s Cape fur seals was the first significant outbreak ever found in marine mammals and has been described as a “significant shift in rabies ecology”.

More than 100 cases have been confirmed in South Africa and Namibia since then, raising fears that aggressive rabid seals could infect humans, pets and other wildlife.

Changing patterns in fish stocks caused by the El Nino phenomenon now potentially risk widening the spread, as uninfected seal populations migrate for food and come into contact with rabid colleagues.

Scientists believe warming sea temperatures off Antarctica could send seal populations northwards into Southern African waters, where they could be exposed to rabies.

They could then return to their home waters, taking the virus with them and infecting other seal populations.

News.title: ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality
News.content:
Arsenal 1 Real Betis 3

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

No Saliba a concern

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

News.title: Ebola outbreak outpacing containment effort, WHO chief warns
News.content:
Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no vaccines or treatments, it has been extremely difficult to contain, according to experts on the ground.

“The outbreak is spreading faster than our scale-up of the response, with new cases doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone,” Dr Tedros said on X.

Part of the difficulty is that the virus was circulating undetected for weeks before the outbreak was formally declared in mid-May, leaving health officials even now racing to catch up with the spread.

Prof Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at Africa CDC, told the Telegraph: “It’s mostly the fact we arrived a bit late. It took us some time before we detected this virus outbreak. And when we detected the outbreak, we already had a total of I can say more than 200 suspected cases. It’s been difficult to catch up. That’s where we are.”

While the DRC has a wealth of experience in tackling haemorrhagic fever outbreaks, the effects of that initial delay are still being felt.

Prof Mbala said: “We have some experience dealing with the cases, the labs, the communication, the infection prevention and control.

“We have some experience... But my observation is that we were very slow, and it’s why we’re in this situation.

“We are slow detecting the people, slow responding, we are slow deploying people, we are slow to recruit the community healthcare workers to improve contact tracing, we are slow to deploy the safe burials.”

DRC’s largest outbreak had previously been from 2018 to 2020, when 3,481 cases were recorded.

The West Africa outbreak recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths according to the WHO.

Prof Mbala said insecurity was also severely hampering attempts to curb the virus. The outbreak epicentre is in Ituri province, which has been wracked by ethnic strife for decades and is also home to militias competing to control mining.

He said: “There are many, many mining groups controlling most of the mining places. We have a big issue with those places, because they are places where the response team cannot go.”

Medics and aid workers have also been undermined by violent public distrust of their efforts.

Locals in the area have either doubted the existence of the virus, or have accused health teams of deliberately spreading the infection, or somehow benefiting from it.

More than a dozen health facilities have been set alight and several health workers have been killed.

Prof Mbala said: “The local people, they also sometimes are very upset, because they believe that it’s a kind of a business, and people who are coming here, they are getting a lot of money, [so] don’t want this disease to stop.”

He said he hoped that immunity was starting to rise in some areas and this would start to curb transmission.

However there was also a risk that people fleeing the outbreak would spread the virus further afield.

He said: “The second scenario is the fact we are seeing people moving from the affected area to new areas, to run away from the response team because they do not want to go to the treatment centre.

“And in complicity with their family members living in other areas, they are now the ones who are spreading the disease to new areas

“So we’ll see new places affected because people are moving around from the affected zone to the non-affected zone.”
