“Unfortunately, public trust in the justice system – the police, the Prosecutor’s Office, the courts and other institutions – is now so low that victims, defendants and lawyers increasingly see shaping public opinion as the only way to obtain justice. They then seek to use public pressure to their advantage,” lawyer Londa Toloraia wrote.

In her view, this reflects a profound crisis affecting both citizens and the justice system itself.

“You no longer trust the state, even when it may actually be making a lawful decision.”

Toloraia also raised a number of questions about the arrests of the two girls: What evidence were they based on? Why did they take place 10 months after the murder? And why were they carried out at night, when Georgian law restricts procedural actions during nighttime hours, particularly in cases involving minors?

“How much influence does public opinion have over the justice system? A great deal. It is extremely difficult to withstand public pressure. And where institutions are fully politicised, it becomes virtually impossible to make a decision that is unpopular with the public,” she argued.

She stressed that legal standards must be upheld even when dealing with those accused of serious crimes – especially when the defendants are minors.

The Avaliani case has also exposed a darker side of public reaction. Following Nia Imnadze’s arrest, social media was flooded with hostile comments directed at both her and her family. Many users described her as the main culprit and called for severe punishment. Others went further, posting comments about the suffering they believed awaited her in prison.

A second group of social media users expressed concern about the tone of those comments. Toloraia addressed the debate in a lengthy social media post.

“Children are not born criminals. Before demanding that they be lynched, we should first ask why they became who they are,” she wrote, adding that juvenile crime in Georgia has reached one of its highest levels in recent years. She argued that the state’s response has focused on opening a “special prison” for children rather than preventing youth crime. A state in which parents who have lost a child must seek justice through public mobilisation, while institutions make decisions according to fluctuations in public pressure, is a broken state,” Toloraia concluded.

World.title: Odesa in summer 2026: Life between sea and war. VIDEO
World.content:
Beaches, bomb-damaged homes and explosions in broad daylight. In the summer of 2026, Odesa is caught between its traditional seaside resort atmosphere and the constant threat of Russian attacks. While some people relax by the sea and stroll through the city centre, others sift through the rubble left by the latest strike.

JAMnews visited Odesa to show what life in the city looks like today.

Odesa and the surrounding region remain frequent targets of Russian strikes. Residential neighbourhoods, critical infrastructure and port facilities have all come under attack.

Russia has carried out combined attacks using drones and missiles, seeking to overwhelm Ukraine‘s air defence systems.

The impact of these attacks is visible across the city. Residential buildings have been damaged, windows blown out and flats destroyed. Strikes have also hit Odesa’s historic centre, including heritage buildings and universities.

Ports in Odesa Region, along with the logistics hubs and warehouses that support them, are also regularly targeted. Attacks on port infrastructure have disrupted Ukraine’s transport network and Black Sea export routes.

The strikes often occur in broad daylight, when the streets are busy, cafés and shops are open, and beaches are filled with residents and visitors. At any moment, the familiar sounds of the city can be interrupted by explosions, air defence fire or the buzz of attack drones.

On several occasions, missiles have been intercepted directly over the coastline while beaches were crowded with people.

Today, it is possible to spend the day at the beach and the night in a bomb shelter.

World.title: Armenia’s growing number of large families: Statistics, one couple’s story and expert insights
World.content:
Surge in large families in Armenia

In recent years, more young families in Armenia have chosen to have a third or even fourth child. According to the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, around 8,300 third and subsequent children were born in 2018. By 2023, that figure had risen to more than 12,400, before easing slightly to around 12,000 in 2024. Overall, the number of third and subsequent births increased by about 45% between 2018 and 2024. Full-year data for 2025 are not yet available, although figures up to September show that 8,070 third and subsequent children had been born.

Experts cite a range of reasons why families choose to have larger families. Conversations with parents of three or more children suggest there is no single explanation, but the most common responses include: “Two children didn’t feel enough“, “We wanted a child of the opposite sex“, and “We were thinking about the country’s future.”

“We planned to have a large family, regardless of state support”

Vanuհi and Tigran married in 2013. For seven years, they were unable to have children. Eventually, they turned to in vitro fertilisation (IVF). In 2021, they became parents to triplets – a girl and two boys.

“We were asked how many children we wanted. We could have chosen one or two. But we decided to take the risk and become parents of triplets, even though we knew the risks were higher,” Vanuhi says.

Parents celebrate their triplets’ birthday.

According to Vanuhi, both she and her husband grew up in large families. From the outset, they wanted a big family of their own – at least three children and, ideally, as many as six.

“I received so much love and care from my brothers and sisters that I found it hard to imagine a family with just one or two children. My parents are no longer alive, but I feel stronger and more complete because I have my brothers and sisters,” says Tigran Hovakimyan.

The couple raised the triplets on their own, without relying on grandparents or other relatives. When the children turned three, they started nursery. Then came another surprise: Vanuhi became pregnant with their fourth child.

Vanuhi says they were astonished, as doctors had told them they had virtually no chance of conceiving naturally.

“We now have four young children. We both work and can provide them with good food, clothes and opportunities for leisure. We also receive state benefits. Because we had triplets, the government counts each of them as a third child and pays 50,000 drams (about $137) per child each month. We now receive an additional 50,000 drams for our fourth child, as well as 30,000 drams (about $82) because my wife is temporarily unable to work while on maternity leave,” Tigran explains.

He says that part of the money is deposited into savings accounts opened in the children’s names, while the rest is spent on their activities and recreation. The family has bought a large inflatable swimming pool for the garden of their home, as well as bicycles, and the children also attend paid extracurricular classes and sports clubs.

Family vacation.

The couple are also setting aside modest savings to help ensure all four children can receive a good education.

“You know, many families have children because of state benefits or other government support. We don’t judge them, but our story is different. We always planned to have three or more children without relying on state assistance. It wasn’t something that influenced our decision. In the early years of our marriage, both my wife and I worked several jobs at the same time so that we could afford to buy a large house, hoping one day we’d have a big family,” Tigran says.

“If we were still paying off a mortgage, we would probably depend on the child benefits that families receive until their children turn six,” Vanuhi adds.

How state encourages higher birth rates

In 2022, Armenia introduced a state support programme under which families receive a monthly payment of 50,000 drams ($137) for a third and each subsequent child until the child reaches the age of six.

By 2025, more than 45,000 children were covered by the scheme.

Under a separate programme, the state repays part of a family’s mortgage principal following the birth of a child. The subsidy amounts to:

up to 500,000 drams ($1,377) for a second child,

for a second child, up to 1 million drams ($2,754) for a third child,

for a third child, up to 1.5 million drams ($4,132) for a fourth child.

The scheme applies to mortgages that meet certain social eligibility criteria and is regarded as one of the government’s key measures to encourage higher birth rates.

In addition, amendments to Armenia’s Labour Code that came into force in 2026 introduced new benefits for working parents. In particular, parents with children under the age of 12 are now entitled to a “parental hour” – a shorter working day without any reduction in pay:

parents with one or two children can finish work 30 minutes earlier;parents with three or more children are entitled to a one-hour reduction in their working day.

The benefit can be used by either the mother or the father.

Families also receive a one-off payment of 500,000 drams ($1,377) for every child, including their first.

More recently, the government approved a new housing programme for families raising six or more children under the age of 18, an initiative proposed by the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs.

“Under this programme, large families will be able to purchase property or build a detached house in any regional community in Armenia with 100% state funding,” ministry spokesperson Gayane Karagezyan said.

The programme does not cover property purchases in Yerevan, however, reflecting the government’s policy of promoting balanced regional development.

“More targeted measures are needed”

Demographer Rubina Grigoryan says the government’s efforts to encourage larger families have produced some results. While the increase in births is evident, she believes it is still not enough.

“New, more targeted programmes are needed. They should be tailored separately for Yerevan and the regions. They should also go beyond financial assistance. The recently introduced ‘parental hour’ is one example of an effective incentive. I believe more should be done to expand access to nurseries and kindergartens. Just look at how many private childcare centres cater for children under the age of two. If the state increased the number of places in public childcare facilities, more women would consider having additional children.”

Grigoryan says attitudes towards large families have also become more positive in recent years. They are not only receiving greater state support but are also more valued by society.

“However, many of these families may face difficulties once their children grow older, particularly with the costs of education and other financial pressures. State support is available only until children reach the age of six. After that, families seem to be left without much assistance. This is something policymakers should also address. As for the recent rise in birth rates, I see one particularly significant factor. The increase in births between 2021 and 2023 was largely influenced by the aftermath of the Karabakh war. Many families decided to have children after the war, each for their own reasons – from a sense of responsibility towards those who died to a desire to help build a stronger country for the future,” Grigoryan says.

World.title: First digital bridge beneath Caspian Sea: How Sumqayit-Aktau cable reshapes Eurasia’s geostrategic landscape
World.content:
Sumqayit-Aktau cable reshapes Eurasia

Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan have completed a key milestone in the implementation of a Caspian Sea project, with the subsea section of the Sumqayit-Aktau Trans-Caspian fibre-optic cable now in place.

The roughly 380-km line is the first fibre-optic infrastructure to be laid on the bed of the Caspian Sea. With a capacity of more than 400 Tbps, the system is being developed by AzerTelecom International and Kazakhtelecom through their joint venture, CaspiLink B.V. The project is being financed entirely by the operators, without any state budget funding.

Offshore works began in July and were completed in early August. The connection of the onshore infrastructure and system testing are scheduled for the autumn, while commercial operations are expected to begin by the end of 2026. The project is more than a technical achievement. As one of the flagship components of Azerbaijan’s Digital Silk Way initiative, it strengthens the digital dimension of the Middle Corridor and has the potential to reshape regional data flows.

Technical and organisational aspects

The capacity of the fibre-optic cable significantly exceeds that of the existing terrestrial routes in the region. This provides the foundation for transmitting large volumes of data and supporting the development of cloud services and future artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The project is being implemented by AzerTelecom International, part of NEQSOL Holding, and Kazakhtelecom through an equal partnership under their joint venture, CaspiLink B.V. Registered in the Netherlands, the company is responsible for both the construction and future operation of the cable. The project is financed entirely with private funds, reducing its exposure to the political and bureaucratic risks associated with state funding. At the same time, its long-term success will depend on the commercial viability of the operators and the stability of the regional political environment.

Laying the cable along the Caspian seabed presented significant technical challenges, as no such operation had previously been carried out there. The route was designed to avoid anchorage areas and military exercise zones. Engineering surveys and environmental approvals were completed in 2025.

The cable was manufactured and tested in China before being shipped to Baku via Kazakhstan’s Kuryk port. Installation was carried out around the clock using a specialised vessel with a displacement of more than 20,000 tonnes. Around 70 specialists took part in the operation. The next phase will involve integrating the onshore landing stations and conducting system tests.

Although commercial operations are scheduled to begin by the end of 2026, the cable’s actual utilisation rates and transit volumes are unlikely to become clear before 2027.

Can Caspian cable provide alternative to Russia and Red Sea routes?

The answer is: to some extent, yes, but not entirely. At present, internet traffic from Central Asia and the South Caucasus largely relies on two main routes: via Russian networks to the north and via the subsea cable systems in the Red Sea and the Mediterranean to the south. In recent years, both have faced geopolitical and infrastructure-related risks, including sanctions, cable damage and network congestion. The Trans-Caspian cable helps reduce this dependence by creating an alternative route that bypasses Russia and Iran, connecting Europe via Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey, or linking eastwards through Kazakhstan to China.

Its impact, however, is unlikely to be immediate or comprehensive. The cable covers only the Aktau-Sumqayit section of the route. A fully functioning digital corridor will also require sufficient terrestrial network capacity in Azerbaijan, Georgia and Kazakhstan, a well-developed network of data centres, and commercial agreements between telecom operators.

From a latency perspective, the Caspian route appears competitive. According to available data, round-trip signal latency between the two shores is around 3.7 milliseconds. However, the extent to which it strengthens digital sovereignty will depend on whether substantial volumes of traffic are rerouted through the new link and whether regional operators gain greater control over traffic routing.

For Central Asian states, the project offers an opportunity to reduce, at least partially, their dependence on Russian transit infrastructure. For the South Caucasus, it strengthens the region’s position as an emerging digital hub. Full digital independence, however, remains a distant prospect, as a significant share of traffic handled by major providers, as well as data flows between China and Europe, will continue to rely on established routes.

Synergy between Middle Corridor and Digital Silk Way

Combining freight transport and digital infrastructure within a single geographic corridor offers practical advantages. The Middle Corridor, or Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, has seen container traffic grow in recent years but continues to face constraints in competing with routes through Russia and other alternative corridors.

Adding a digital dimension makes the corridor more technologically advanced by enabling real-time transmission of logistics data, digitalising customs and border procedures, and accelerating insurance and financial transactions. Azerbaijan’s ambition to become a regional digital hub is closely linked to this synergy. Complementing existing energy pipelines, railways and seaports, the fibre-optic cable enhances the country’s appeal as a transit hub for data flows.

A realistic assessment, however, is warranted. Although Azerbaijan’s geographical location is advantageous, becoming a fully fledged digital hub will require large-scale data centres, affordable electricity, a highly skilled workforce and the presence of international cloud service providers. At present, these conditions have only been partially met. Strengthening terrestrial links with Georgia and Turkey, together with laying additional subsea cables across the Black Sea, would help unlock the full potential of the Digital Silk Way.

For Kazakhstan, further development of Aktau port and the modernisation of the country’s east-west digital infrastructure will be equally important. Ultimately, the benefits of this synergy will depend on both countries developing their respective infrastructure at a comparable pace.

Private funding model and risks

The advantages of delivering the project without state funding are clear. It reduces the risk of delays linked to political decision-making, places commercial incentives at the forefront and makes the project more transparent to international investors. CaspiLink B.V.’s registration in the Netherlands also provides greater legal certainty and a well-established framework for dispute resolution. The main vulnerabilities of the model stem from the financial position of the operators themselves and their political connections.

AzerTelecom is part of NEQSOL Holding, a privately owned business group with significant regional influence. Kazakhtelecom, by contrast, is a telecommunications operator with close ties to the Kazakh state. This ownership structure helps balance political risk: it combines commercial flexibility with the prospect of state support if required. At the same time, political developments in either country, sanctions risks or sharp fluctuations in energy markets could affect the operators’ ability to finance future investment.

The project’s cost was previously estimated at around $50m. Private financing has helped keep investment at a manageable level. However, any future expansion – including a possible extension towards Turkmenistan or an increase in transmission capacity – is likely to require additional capital. Long-term transit agreements and cooperation with international telecommunications consortia will therefore be important in mitigating these risks.

Geopolitical context

For China, the project forms a practical component of the Digital Silk Way, helping diversify data flows between Central Asia and Europe. The cable was manufactured in China and supports Beijing’s broader efforts to expand digital connectivity across Eurasia. For Western countries, meanwhile, the digital dimension of the Middle Corridor is strategically significant as it offers an alternative route that bypasses Russia and Iran.

Against the backdrop of efforts to develop the Middle Corridor and establish new data links between Europe and Asia, the cable takes on added strategic importance. It does not pose direct competition to Russia. Over the longer term, however, reducing Central Asia’s reliance on Russian digital transit infrastructure could weaken Moscow’s influence in the region.

The project’s strategic significance is further enhanced by its parallel development alongside existing energy infrastructure. The Caspian region is already home to major oil and gas export routes, including the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline and the Southern Gas Corridor. Running along the same geographic axis, the fibre-optic cable effectively serves as an “information pipeline”.

This helps diversify the region’s infrastructure and reinforces its role not only as an energy exporter but also as a hub for data transit. At the same time, geopolitical tensions, unresolved issues related to the legal status and security of the Caspian, military activity and sanctions risks remain potential threats to both digital and energy infrastructure.

Prospects and limitations

A possible next step would be to extend the route towards Turkmenistan. A Sumqayit-Turkmenbashi link could become an important component of a fully fledged Digital Silk Way. Its implementation, however, is likely to depend on Ashgabat’s restrictive telecommunications policies and broader strategic priorities.

As data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure expand, Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan could benefit from relatively affordable electricity and favourable conditions for cooling equipment. More broadly, deeper regional integration will depend on agreements between telecom operators, transparent pricing and simpler cross-border procedures.

The project also faces a number of constraints. The Caspian Sea’s fragile environment, potential restrictions linked to military activity, reliance on Chinese equipment and ongoing consolidation in the global telecommunications market could all slow its development. In addition, the cable’s commercial success will ultimately depend on demand. Regional traffic alone may not be sufficient to utilise its full capacity, making it necessary to attract major international data flows.

World.title: Armenia begins shift from Russia towards EU – but finish line remains distant
World.content:
Armenia between Europe and Russia

Against this backdrop, the European Union pledged to “stand by Armenia”. EU leaders have already announced tens of millions of dollars in financial assistance and opened the bloc’s markets to Armenian goods that had suddenly ceased to meet Russian quality standards. More importantly, Brussels has expressed interest in further deepening ties with Yerevan, while Armenia’s re-elected leadership says the election results demonstrate the public’s desire to continue along the country’s European path.

Parliamentary elections in Armenia are over, but the political—and geopolitical—debate continues. Many viewed the vote as a de facto referendum on the country’s future orientation: Russia or the European Union.During the election campaign, Moscow imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian food products, a move widely interpreted in Armenia as an attempt to influence public opinion. Contrary to some expectations, Russia not only kept those trade restrictions in place after the election but tightened them.

JAMnews reviewed the latest developments and spoke to analysts with opposing views. Residents of Armenia also shared their opinions on how they believe the country should shape its future.

Yerevan residents rush to work in the morning. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

How Armenia’s pivot took shape

Few people remember now, but immediately after the 2018 “Velvet Revolution”, led by then-opposition figure and now Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, he insisted that his government would not pursue any geopolitical realignment. At the time, Armenia was already a member of the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). Years later, speaking from podiums in both Europe and Yerevan, the same Pashinyan has declared Armenia’s aspiration to join the European Union.

So what happened in between? Over the past several years, the entire security architecture of the South Caucasus has unraveled, triggering a snowball effect. Initially, relations between Yerevan and Moscow developed without major friction. Then came the 2020 Karabakh war. Armenia was defeated and ceased to be the guarantor of Nagorno-Karabakh’s security. Formally, Yerevan had no grounds to hold Moscow responsible in 2020. Nagorno-Karabakh was not part of Armenia, and the agreements signed between the two countries applied only to Armenia itself, not to the unrecognised entity.

However, events then took an unexpected turn.

Over the following two years, Azerbaijan launched several military operations on Armenia’s internationally recognised territory. Yerevan appealed to its allies in the CSTO for assistance, but received neither military support nor even a political assessment of the situation.

The allies responded that it was first necessary to establish where exactly the escalation had taken place, arguing that the Armenia-Azerbaijan border had not been formally delimited. Pashinyan replied sharply:

“To say that there is no border between Armenia and Azerbaijan is to claim that the Collective Security Treaty Organization has no area of responsibility. And if there is no area of responsibility, then there is no organisation.”

Since then, Yerevan, finding itself alone in the face of what it viewed as an external security threat, has frozen its participation in the CSTO and turned increasingly towards Europe. According to some analysts, the price of that shift was Armenia’s official recognition of Nagorno-Karabakh as part of Azerbaijan. In return, the European Union deployed a civilian monitoring mission to Armenia, which helped stabilise the situation along the border with Azerbaijan. Armenia also secured the EU’s political backing.

Retiree Andrey Karapetyan shares his views on European integration. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

Shift gathered pace

These developments on the ground were inevitably followed by political change. The entire Armenia-Azerbaijan negotiation process shifted to Western platforms—an outcome few had anticipated. Since the conflict began in the 1990s, Moscow had served as the principal mediator and facilitator of the peace talks.

Following the events of September 2023, when Azerbaijan’s one-day military operation prompted the entire Armenian population to flee Nagorno-Karabakh, Russia effectively lost its influence in the region.

At the same time, Russia also lost its standing among much of Armenia’s population, no longer being viewed as a friendly state.

A park in Yerevan, where locals gather to play backgammon and discuss politics. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

Although Russia formally remains Armenia’s strategic ally, many Armenians have not forgotten that Russian peacekeepers effectively acted as bystanders, failing to fulfil their mission of protecting the Armenian population of Nagorno-Karabakh. Following the CSTO’s refusal to defend Armenia’s territorial integrity, relations between Moscow and Yerevan cooled even further. The Armenian leadership also adopted a more outspoken tone towards Russia, both in its rhetoric and in its actions.

At the same time, contacts between the Armenian government and its European partners intensified. Brussels allocated hundreds of millions of dollars to support political and economic reforms in Armenia, as well as strengthen the country’s borders. France also began supplying Armenia with military equipment. The culmination of these developments came on 17 October 2023, when speaking at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan declared:

“The Republic of Armenia is ready to be as close to the European Union as the European Union considers possible. Our joint statement with President von der Leyen says: ‘In these difficult times, the EU and Armenia stand shoulder to shoulder.'”

In the years that followed, Pashinyan repeatedly stated that Armenia would seek EU membership. The parliamentary elections held in June and their outcome only reinforced the government’s determination.

“Last year, we adopted a law launching the process of accession to the European Union, which, I would remind you, was initiated by civil society. I believe this provides an additional incentive to give new momentum to our democratic and institutional reforms so that we can achieve EU standards as quickly as possible.

This is our main intermediate goal because we understand that no country can become a full member of the European Union without meeting its standards. Therefore, our primary task is first and foremost to comply with EU standards. […]If we are admitted to the European Union, we will be happy. If we are not, we will still benefit, because Armenia will have become a country that meets European standards, with all the positive consequences that entails,” Pashinyan said at the time.

System administrator Artak Gaboyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

Russia pushes back

At the start of the crisis in Armenian-Russian relations, Moscow responded relatively cautiously to Yerevan’s efforts to move closer to Europe. The Kremlin sought to avoid further destabilising the situation, citing Armenia’s difficult historical circumstances. Even Armenia’s effective suspension of its participation in the CSTO did not result in a fundamental reassessment of bilateral relations.

However, Moscow appeared to change its approach in the run-up to the parliamentary elections held in June.

One of the defining moments came during Pashinyan’s meeting with Vladimir Putin in Moscow in April, when the Russian president openly asked him to allow pro-Russian political forces to participate in the elections. He was primarily referring to Russian-Armenian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. However, as Karapetyan holds citizenship of several countries, not only Armenia, Armenian law bars him from serving as an MP or becoming prime minister. Pashinyan reportedly made this clear to Putin.

The Kremlin nevertheless continued to support pro-Russian political figures while also taking more concrete steps. Russian regulators began imposing restrictions on imports of Armenian products. Initially, the measures targeted specific companies and categories of goods, but they were later expanded to cover almost all agricultural produce from Armenia.

Businessman Suren Margaryan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

The situation continued to escalate. Armenian officials began openly accusing Moscow of attempting to interfere in the country’s internal affairs and engineer a change of government.

At the same time, international media reported on alleged hybrid attacks against Armenia. Reuters also published a report alleging that the Kremlin had devised a plan to bring 100,000 Armenian citizens into the country to vote for pro-Russian political forces.

Following the elections, Moscow has stepped up its calls for Armenia to decide, once and for all, which direction it intends to take. Russian officials have specifically called for a referendum on whether the country should pursue integration with the European Union or the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), arguing that choosing the EU would require Armenia to leave the EAEU.

“No one is pushing Armenia out of the EAEU. They themselves have said they want to join the European Union. They need to make a choice. And the sooner that choice is made, the better it will be for everyone,” Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksey Overchuk said.

This culminated in a joint statement by the EAEU member states calling for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership.

Central Yerevan. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

Armenia says time is not right for referendum

In response to Moscow’s demands, the Armenian authorities say they have no plans to hold a referendum or withdraw from the EAEU—for now. The key word is “for now.” Yerevan intends to remain a member of the EAEU until there is a realistic prospect of joining the European Union. Moreover, under the EAEU’s founding rules, Armenia cannot be expelled from the bloc without its consent.

However, holding a referendum on EU membership appears to be a realistic prospect in the longer term. Opinion polls also suggest such a referendum could succeed. Since the 2020 war, Russia’s popularity in Armenia has declined markedly, while support for European integration has continued to grow.

According to a survey conducted by the International Republican Institute (IRI) in May 2026, 75% of Armenians support the country’s accession to the European Union, while 58% say they would vote in favour of joining the bloc in a referendum. The findings point to a sustained decline in trust in Russia and growing pro-European sentiment among the Armenian public.

Photographer Mane Sergoyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

What do experts say?

Which direction should Armenia take? That is arguably the country’s defining question today. Does Armenia have the capacity to make a definitive choice in favour of the European Union? How might Russia respond if it does? And what security risks could such a shift entail?

Political analyst Robert Gevondyan says Yerevan is pursuing a diversification of its foreign policy, a goal repeatedly articulated by the country’s leadership. In his view, this aligns with the interests of Armenia’s European partners.

“Armenia is already receiving a certain level of support, particularly through its cooperation with France. It is possible that, in the future, security cooperation will expand to include other countries, although there is not yet enough information at this stage to identify them. At the same time, it should be remembered that the EU operates under NATO’s security umbrella. While Armenia is not currently seeking rapid accession to the Alliance, if it succeeds in developing close ties with individual EU member states, it could gain access to additional opportunities as an indirect beneficiary of NATO’s resources,” he said.

Is Armenia ready to become part of the European Union today? Gevondyan argues that the question itself is misplaced, as every country must go through a lengthy accession process before joining the bloc.

“No country is ever fully prepared to begin the integration process overnight. By the time Armenia is ready, it will effectively already be part of Europe. States usually go through a long period of integration, during which they implement reforms across various sectors, align with European standards, improve product quality and reach agreements on mutual trade. This process takes years. Armenia is ready to embark on that journey. At the same time, it is impossible to reconcile EU requirements and the conditions for trading with the West with the standards and requirements that exist within the EAEU. We are only at the beginning of a long road.”

Journalist Marianna Mkrtchyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

“Armenia is still a long way from joining the European Union. But the current trajectory could already result in serious losses—not only economically, but also in terms of the country’s sovereignty,” argues political commentator Hayk Khalatyan, founder of the Analytical Centre for Strategic Studies and Initiatives.

Khalatyan also argues that the Armenian leadership will ultimately be unable to sustain its current course of deepening ties with the European Union while remaining a member of the EAEU:

“Pashinyan’s challenge now, after the elections, is to try to normalise relations with Moscow. He will be expected to take concrete steps demonstrating that he is abandoning his previous foreign policy course. But that would effectively mean turning his back on the powerful external actors who helped him remain in power. The question, then, is which path he will choose: to turn his back on the West and Turkey, or continue down the path of confrontation with Russia and the gradual breakdown of bilateral relations. I very much doubt that Pashinyan will abandon his Western partners and move towards normalising ties with Russia. He would like to preserve the policy he has pursued in recent years—reaping the economic benefits of EAEU membership while, in practice, steadily distancing Armenia politically from Russia. But we are now seeing that Moscow is no longer willing to tolerate that approach.”

Human rights activist and film director Hovhannes Ishkhanyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan.

At the same time, relations between Brussels and Moscow remain deeply confrontational, with some political and security circles even discussing the possibility of a future conflict between Russia and the West.

Whatever the outcome, Armenia is now adapting to a new geopolitical reality while facing Russian trade restrictions. The country is seeking to redirect its exports towards European markets and diversify its trade partners. If it succeeds, Yerevan will remove what many see as its last major economic dependency on Russia.

Yasha Solomonyan, chairman of the Armenian Association of Professional Guides, shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

With the support of the Russian Language News Exchange

World.title: UK embassy in Georgia: Amaglobeli’s sentence ‘disproportionate’ and politically motivated
World.content:
UK embassy condemns Amaglobeli’s sentence

The UK embassy in Georgia has described the sentence handed down to journalist Mzia Amaglobeli as disproportionate and politically motivated, and has called for her immediate release.

“A year ago today Mzia Amaglobeli, a prominent Georgian journalist, was sentenced to two years in prison. We remain concerned that her sentence is disproportionate and politicised and call again for her immediate release,” the embassy’s post on Facebook read.

Mzia Amaglobeli was sentenced on 6 August 2025.

The journalist was arrested on 11 January 2025 on charges of assaulting Batumi police chief Irakli Dgebuadze. On 14 January, Batumi City Court granted the prosecution’s request to remand her in custody pending trial.

The defence’s requests to have the pre-trial detention measure changed were rejected by the courts. Batumi City Court ruled the request inadmissible, while on 19 February 2025 Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld the decision to keep Amaglobeli in pre-trial detention.

According to Nona Kurdovanidze, chair of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association, the court relied on a falsified protocol when justifying her pre-trial detention.

Following her arrest, Mzia Amaghlobeli went on a hunger strike that lasted 38 days. On 18 February 2025, it was announced that she had ended the hunger strike and resumed eating under medical supervision.

World.title: AFL issues Cats a 'please explain' over defender's concussion contract
World.content:
Geelong has been handed a belated 'please explain' notice from the AFL after initially avoiding sanction over its controversial secret deal with defender Jake Kolodjashnij, a player with a history of concussions.

In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij, who on Friday evening identified himself as the player in question, whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action down the line.

The bombshell concussion case emerged on Thursday and pressure mounted on the league and Geelong after the AFL didn't hand down any punishment that night.

On Friday afternoon, Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking said he had signed off on the deal and confirmed the 'please explain' notice.

Geelong's Steve Hocking said the club would provide information to the AFL about Kolodjashnij's contract. (AAP Image: Erik Anderson)

"I take responsibility for the fact that we didn't lodge it with the AFL and the (AFL)PA," Hocking told reporters in Geelong.

"… I have received a letter of 'please explain' from the AFL in relation to this matter, so we'll deal with that over the coming days."

Hocking said not registering the deal was a "misstep" and was uncertain what consequences Geelong would face.

"We've got a 'please explain' letter, and at the appropriate time we'll work through that with the AFL," he said.

"We'll have to respond to that, and then it'll be up to the AFL, and whatever that is, we'll accept."

Later on Friday, Kolodjashnij issued a statement through Geelong, confirming he was the previously unnamed player.

"While I appreciate the efforts made not to identify me, the speculation has left me feeling I needed to address this personally," Kolodjashnij said.

"I participated fully in the AFL's independent concussion panel process, respected its independence, and was comfortable with the outcome. I have continued playing AFL football since.

"What disappoints me most is that my private medical information has been made public. Everyone deserves the right to keep their confidential medical information private.

"… I am healthy, feeling good, and focused on playing my role for the team for the remainder of the season."

The 2022 premiership defender, 30, has played 209 games.

Kolodjashnij's twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, retired prematurely in 2020 due to concussion.

On Thursday night, calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL had insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

Geelong also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

Grief-stricken mother of star footballer reveals AFL executive phone call West Coast Eagles star Adam Hunter's mother Joanne Brown says AFL executive Laura Kane reached out to her, but the grieving mother says the phone call was "too little, too late".

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board when the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the AFL statement.

Drummond did not front the media and issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Many AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and former number one draft pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham 'Polly' Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multimillion-dollar concussion class action against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Deliberately misleading party name approved for Victorian election
World.content:
The Victorian Electoral Commissioner has urged voters to do their research before casting their ballot, after a party with a deliberately misleading name was successfully registered ahead of the November election.

This week a group wanting to register a political party called the "Free Palestine Party" was knocked back because a pro-Israel activist had already registered a party called "Free Palestine".

Electoral Commissioner Sven Bluemmel said the risk of voters being duped by the registered party's name was not a matter for the VEC under state laws.

"The law requires us to register a party once they meet all the criteria under the law and that was the case here," he said.

"The criteria do not go to what the policy position of the party is, that's not for me to decide."

He said he could only decide whether a party name was considered offensive, too long or resembled the name of an existing registered political party, which was the case for "Free Palestine Party".

Victorians will cast their vote in the state election in November. (Supplied: Victorian Electoral Commission)

Student Palestinian activist Ibrahim Hadi, who was the applicant behind the rejected party, said he understood the VEC's decision but it was frustrating.

"[The Free Palestine party's] trying to paint themselves as Palestinian and use the Palestinian identity to poke fun at people that are standing up for the oppressed," he said.

Mr Bluemmel said it was important voters used the information available to them to educate themselves before voting.

"As a voter, do that research, find out what the party stands for, find out what the candidate stands for and always come to the VEC's website to see who's registered, who's behind it. That's all publicly available," he said.

The group voting system allows the selected party to distribute preferences how it pleases. (ABC News: Freya Michie)

Group voting system before parliament

"Free Palestine" was registered by Melbourne-based YouTuber, Avi Yemini, who has previously served in Israel's military and has heavily criticised pro-Palestine rallies.

Earlier this year Mr Yemini posted a social media video calling for 750 Victorians to become members so he could register the party with the electoral commission.

One of the requirements to register a new party is to have at least 500 members who are enrolled to vote in Victoria and are not members of another registered political party.

Mr Yemini has previously said by registering "Free Palestine" he wanted to redirect left-wing votes towards parties on the right.

Avi Yemini previously said his intention was to redistribute votes from left-wing parties to conservatives. (Supplied: Rebel News)

It is made possible because Victoria currently has a group voting system — although it is unlikely to still be in place by November's election.

The group voting system sees most voters select a single party "above the line" and in doing so, whether the voter realises it or not, they hand over all their decisions about preference allocations to that party.

Victoria is the only jurisdiction that still has this system, but a law is currently before the parliament to abolish the controversial feature.

Whilst he would not be drawn on the merits of the group voting system, Mr Bluemmel said abolishing it would bring Victoria in line with other jurisdictions.

"For me, the main consideration is if we're going to get change the sooner it happens the better because we need to prepare," he said.

Mr Bluemmel said based on data the VEC collects, "Australia has a very strong, trusted electoral system".

"Victoria is no exception to that, but we can't take that for granted. We mustn't take that for granted," he said.

World.title: In a town families are moving to, an important health service has departed
World.content:
Leanna Testa was at a mother's group in the outback town of Longreach, in Western Queensland, when she heard about the help other women were receiving for post-birthing issues.

"I was talking to a few mums at the Feral Mums Club about it, just wanting to know with ab[dominal] separation, what I'm dealing with, if it's severe or if it's minor," Ms Testa said.

"One of the mums told me that there was a lady [pelvic floor physiotherapist] out here and that she is amazing."

Leanna Testa was referred to see the pelvic health physiotherapist in Longreach in May, but never heard back. (ABC Western Queensland: Jay Carstrens)

The mother of two children obtained a referral to see the specialist.

"That was back in May, and to this day I've never received a phone call," Ms Testa said.

The Central West's only trained public pelvic floor physiotherapist left the region in July after spending a couple of years based at Longreach Hospital.

One of her previous patients said access to the treatment locally was life-changing.

"She gave me the ability just to function without pain, like just everyday, day-to-day, walking up the stairs, getting in and out of the car," mother of two Antje Dekruyf said.

Jade Miller says she faces an eight-hour drive to see a pelvic health physiotherapist in Rockhampton. (ABC Western Queensland: Jay Carstens)

New resident Jade Miller said she was facing an eight-hour drive to get help with her abdominal separation.

"I did my initial appointment in Rockhampton [before I moved], but because there is no other specialist out here, I can't have any follow-up appointments," Ms Miller said.

"If I do [need an appointment], I have to go back to Rockhampton, which is not really doable with two young children."

Now, women across the Central West face uncertainty about access to specialised care for conditions including birth injury, endometriosis and menopause.

Recruitment underway, specialty skill not guaranteed

Hospital data reveals a growth in the number of births in Longreach, rising by 60 per cent between 2020 and 2025, from 54 to 86 per year, reflecting a community view that the number of families in the region had increased.

Amid the outback baby boom, the Central West Hospital and Health Service (CWHHS) said in a statement it rejected any suggestion it was downgrading pelvic health services.

The Central West Hospital and Health Service says specialist allied health professionals are in short supply. (ABC Western Queensland: Jay Carstens)

"Across Queensland and indeed Australia, allied health clinicians with specialist skills are in short supply and extremely difficult to attract and retain in remote areas, including the Central West," executive director of regional health Craig Carey said.

The CWHHS director said recruitment for a generalist physiotherapist was underway, but he could not guarantee they would have the same level of pelvic health experience as their predecessor.

Longreach has a population of about 3,000 people. (ABC Western Qld: Jay Carstens)

Pelvic Pain Australia's vice chair Alexandra Diggles, who is also a physiotherapist pelvic floor specialist, said that was concerning.

"A generalist physio in a hospital may never have covered or understood any pelvic health concerns," Ms Diggles said.

"Not even attempting to replace that position with a needed service may be a bit of a shortfall of innovation or insight for that health service as well."

Several mothers at local playgroups say they have needed help from a pelvic health physiotherapist. (ABC Western Queensland: Jay Carstens)

It is that potential gap in future services that has local mothers worried.

"When you're dealing with pelvic floor and having to do internal exams, I think it's really important for someone to be very knowledgeable in that area," Ms Dekruyf.

"I wouldn't personally feel comfortable with a generalist [without training] doing that sort of stuff."

Growing industry interest

Pelvic Pain Australia said the role of physiotherapy in managing pelvic pain symptoms was a growing specialty.

"Physios are known for improving muscle function … [especially during] the transition times in life like pregnancy or menopause or after prostate surgery, when there's been a challenge to that system," Ms Diggles said.

The Australian Physiotherapy Association said more physiotherapists were choosing to upskill in women's health, which could ease rural shortages.

The organisation said since launching pelvic health training courses in 2020, 669 physiotherapists had gained the knowledge required for after-birth treatment.

"Women in rural areas shouldn't have to choose between living in the community that they love and having access to the physiotherapy services that they deserve," the organisation's member director Catherine Willis said.

Antje Dekruyf says Longreach is a growing town and deserves to have better specialist services. (ABC Western Queensland: Jay Carstens)

That is something Ms Dekruyf agrees with.

"I think with the growing number of families, it's a necessity, especially because Longreach is the hub [of the West]," she said.

World.title: After 67 years, Brisbane's Centenary Pool to close for major Olympic upgrade
World.content:
Brisbane's historic Centenary Pool will close at the end of August to undergo major redevelopment for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in 2032.

The now heritage-listed pool was first opened to the public in 1959 and became Brisbane's first Olympic standard pool.

The centre reflected a national mania for swimming in the wake of Australia's success in the pool at the 1956 Melbourne Olympic Games, where the host country walked away with eight gold medals in swimming events.

A busy day at the Centenary Pool seen from above. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

The pool was designed by Brisbane City's architect James Birrel.

Mr Birrel passed away in 2019, but his son Jack Birrell, now a Tasmanian-based architect himself, has fond memories of the pool.

"I can actually remember as a child, Dad holding my hand and walking me through the project," Mr Birrell said.

Loading...

"He talked a lot about how his role as a city architect, how he had a sort of ethical and moral obligation to make public buildings not just financially stack up but to be the most they can possibly be for all people."

With its distinctive restaurant "floating" above the water, Mr Birrel said Centenary Pool was a "cultural mecca" in its heyday.

The restaurant above the pool was a popular spot for wedding receptions. (Supplied: Brisbane City Archives)

"All the dignitaries of the day would be seen there, it was a real place to promenade and look out over the world."

Childhood memories

Donna Hansen, 67, grew up in Brisbane's northern suburbs and said she would visit the pool "two or three times a week" in summer as a child.

"We would go from when it opened to when it closed, the whole day," she said.

Swimmers enjoying the Centenary Pool (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

"It was amazing. It was the walk back to the bus stop we all hated, but it was a really good part of my childhood."

Allana French has been coming to the pool for about 40 years.

Ms French said she could recall a distinctive smell from when an Indian restaurant operated at the pool during the 70s and 80s.

"I can remember when you would take a breath and you could smell curries coming from the restaurant."

Fresh from the water, Allana French said she has been visiting Centenary Pool for about 40 years. (ABC News: Stephen Clarke)

Greg Mahony, 79, used to visit as a schoolboy on Saturdays.

"It was all good fun, jumping off the high tower. I tried to teach myself a bit so I wouldn't be embarrassed at the annual swimming carnival," he said.

" All the young ones would be there and get out of the pool and sunbake on the concrete. "

On September 1 the centre will be handed over to the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA), the body responsible for delivering the venue infrastructure for the 2032 Games.

Centenary Pool will form part of the new National Aquatic Centre, which will include three new pools and permanent seating for 8,800 attendees.

Centenary Pool's diving tower inspires memories of terror and excitement in equal measures. (Supplied: Brisbane City Archives)

Mr Mahony said he hopes the site remains a community swimming pool while also helping to "continue Australia's swimming domination".

Olympian Mark Stockwell won three medals for Australia in swimming at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympic Games.

He was instrumental in pushing for a redevelopment of the pool in the 1990s and just a few years later the centre was listed on Queensland's Heritage Register.

Olympic swimmer Mark Stockwell. (ABC News: Cameron Lang)

He hopes the pool will continue to be looked after and preserved for the community as it enters the "third stage of its life".

"It was a gift from the Queensland government to the Brisbane City Council and to the people of Brisbane for its centenary back in 1959," he said.

"I think that's an important history, and it's an important thing to preserve."

World.title: Madonna and Blur producer William Orbit dies aged 69
World.content:
Grammy Award-winning British musician and producer William Orbit, who worked with artists including Madonna, Britney Spears and U2, has died aged 69, his family and friends said on Friday.

The London-born musician, who won two of his three Grammys for production work on Madonna's 1998 album Ray Of Light, died at home on July 23, according to their statement posted on his Instagram page.

"We are deeply saddened by his passing. He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness," it stated.

As well as helping Madonna move into electronica and trip-hop with the 1998 hit album, Orbit also worked with the US star on 2000's Music as well as co-writing and performing on her 1999 single Beautiful Stranger.

The track, which appeared in the second Austin Powers film, earned him another Grammy for best song written for visual media.

Orbit was also nominated for Grammys for his work on Pink's song Feel Good Time, his own 2000 album Pieces In A Modern Style and for record of the year for Ray Of Light.

He also produced for Britpop band Blur, girl group All Saints and Spice Girl Mel C.

She paid tribute to Orbit on Instagram, posting that it was "such an honour to have worked with this great man".

Meanwhile Nicole Appleton of All Saints posted: "He was a treasure in the music industry and we had the most amazing times in the studio and socially. We will forever celebrate him as a music icon."

Orbit also worked with Britney Spears and will.i.am on the 2013 album Britney Jean and produced two songs that featured on U2's compilation The Best Of 1990–2000.

He had a solo career which produced 12 studio albums, largely electronic music, and was also a member of the groups Bassomatic and Torch Song.

AFP

World.title: Landowners still rebuilding a year after deepest snowfall in 'living memory'
World.content:
When New South Wales Northern Tablelands residents woke up to a snowfall last August, they couldn't have imagined they would still be cleaning up 12 months on.

The snow closed roads, cut power and felled branches and fences across swathes of the region.

Although the Bureau of Meteorology does not have official records of alpine snowfalls and snow depth, it was reported at the time that snowfalls of up to 20 to 40 centimetres were seen in areas such as Guyra, Walcha and Armidale.

There was widespread damage at Greenhill Orchards with netting collapsing over multiple hectares. (Supplied: Greenhill Orchards)

Warren Yeomans, the sixth generation to run his family's fruit orchard at Arding, said the snow was unlike anything he had seen before.

"The snow event itself was once in a lifetime; it was far bigger than any other known in living memory."

Slow and tedious work

The Yeomans' family orchard has been operating for more than 160 years, growing cherries, apples, pears and more.

Mr Yeomans said the snow extensively damaged their netted orchards, with the estimated cost about half a million dollars.

The Yeomans' orchard was hit with "unprecedented" damage one year ago when snow carpeted the Northern Tablelands. (ABC News: Brigitte Murphy)

"It [the snow] collapsed all of our structures as well as a lot of native timber, which is still an ongoing process in cleaning up.

"Literally cutting net off the structure which was all over the place, we removed all the net, then all the wires and cables, undoing clips and things which there are thousands of.

Warren Yeomans says he has never seen anything like the 2025 snowstorm and hopes he does not again. (Supplied: Greenhill Orchards)

" It's a long process of physical labour. We are moving forwards but it's starting from a long way back. "

Mr Yeomans said the impact from the snowstorm on their business, Greenhill Orchards, was being felt this season and possibly would be for years to come.

One year later some netting at Greenhill Orchards is back in place but trees are still recovering. (ABC News: Brigitte Murphy)

"We had a very low crop this year because of the tree damage … they had to recover and get their root systems back in place so we had a significantly reduced crop."

Community steps in to help

A natural disaster declaration by the state government covered 10 local government areas, including Armidale and Uralla.

Assistance included grants for low-income uninsured residents and concessional interest rate loans for small businesses, primary producers and non-profit organisations.

The Yeomans family is still repairing damage from the snowstorm 12 months on. (Supplied: Greenhill Orchards)

"We were able to apply for a low-interest loan but that's been a long and arduous task," Mr Yeomans said.

He said there was still a lot of work to do on the orchard in the long term.

The recovery from 2025's snowstorm is still underway at Greenhill Orchards. (ABC News: Brigitte Murphy)

"We're probably halfway through getting our structures back in place.

" It was a disaster in slow motion and the recovery seems to be the same sort of thing. It's in slow motion too. "

Slipping through the cracks

The Kindly Animal Sanctuary cares for more than 250 animals, including donkeys, camels and cattle. (ABC News: Brigitte Murphy)

Less than 30 kilometres north of the orchard is the Kindly Animal Sanctuary.

Trinity Hooper and her mother Naomi call the sanctuary home alongside the countless chickens, cattle, donkeys, pigs and even camels they care for.

The not-for-profit was also inundated with snow, leaving many animals confused and cold.

Ms Hooper said her mother spent hours in the snow.

As the day progressed snow continued to blanket the property resulting in near white-out weather conditions. (Supplied: Kindly Animal Sanctuary)

"She walked the 350 acres multiple times throughout those couple of days, carting food and water to every single animal.

"So much work and every time you turned around there was another animal behind you that shouldn't be there because a tree had fallen on their fence.

" We literally did not own a single fence that didn't have a tree on it. "

One year on from the snowstorm Trinity Hooper and her mother are still a long way off repairing all the damage. (ABC News: Brigitte Murphy)

Ms Hooper said she did not know how much money the repair would cost them, but that it had been an enormous undertaking.

"Just to repair one fence with one tree on it, you're looking at anywhere between $5,000 and $10,000," she said.

" We're still doing it. It's 12 months later and we still have not finished the clean-up. "

The sanctuary had significant damage, including to most of the fencing on the property. (ABC News: Brigitte Murphy)

Ms Hooper said the sanctuary was unsuccessful when applying for grants from the natural disaster declaration.

"I think we do just fall through the cracks because even though we do have the cattle and sheep and things that do tick a lot of those boxes, they're not for commercial use or you don't have primary producer status.

"I think it would be lovely if the government did sit there with a checklist and say, 'Alright, we've helped the farmers, we've helped the community members and we've repaired the school … how about we go out and look at the charities and send them some money, let's send them help.'

World.title: Vulnerable community members push for Census recognition
World.content:
People sleeping rough face many hardships, and completing a Census form is not often a priority.

However, capturing the number and profile of the nation's homeless is important to advocates and government planners.

For several years, home for Timothy Coles has been a tent at the edges of Coffs Harbour.

He said he would complete the Census next week to give information about the hardship that it is faced by Australians.

Timothy Coles will sit down at a homeless crisis service to complete the Census. (ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds)

There is high demand for homeless crisis support at Pete's Place in one of Australia's homeless hotspots, Coffs Harbour in New South Wales.

Run by St Vincent de Paul, Pete's Place offers showers, laundry facilities, tents, food and caseworkers.

Chris Monk receives fresh food from George Ayoub at Pete's Place in Coffs Harbour. (ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds)

Pete's Place team leader Anna Millett said clients faced barriers to completing a full Census form.

"Some of the people who come into our service can't read or write, so it can make filling out a form quite daunting," Ms Millett said.

"We see people with complex issues, such as mental health, drug and alcohol use, people experiencing domestic or family violence and young people," she said.

Census field officers have been at Pete's Place and the Uniting Church Soup Kitchen in Coffs Harbour for the past week to answer questions.

Anna Millett says some clients mistrust the government and Census data protection. (ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds)

"Having a complete understanding of how many people are experiencing homelessness in Australia can inform government policy and how the sector as a whole responds to homelessness," Ms Millett said.

From tomorrow, field officers will interview those willing to participate and record their responses on a custom homeless Census form of just two pages.

Beth Edwards discusses the Census with Ray Webb at the Coffs Harbour Uniting Church Soup Kitchen. (ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds)

Australian Bureau of Statistics Census national spokesperson Emily Walter said the bureau had been working with homeless services much earlier to learn where and how to best gather Census data.

"We've now got in place a strategy where we are in locations where we have known higher populations of people sleeping rough," Ms Walter said.

"We are onsite at support services, where people sleeping rough seek support, so places like soup kitchens [and] streetside medical facilities.

Emily Walter says the bureau has this year worked earlier with agencies serving homeless people. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"Importantly, [we are] working really closely at those locations across Australia during the week of Census, to conduct face-to-face interviews with people sleeping rough."

Australian National University demographer Liz Allen was missed in the 1996 Census count when she was "couch surfing" as a teen, but said more "holistic" ABS definitions now captured that population.

"The Australian Bureau of Statistics has matured in their definition of homelessness and made the collection of data very deliberate and sensitive," Dr Allen said.

Liz Allen's teen experience of homelessness was not captured in the Census that year. (Supplied: Liz Allen)

"This enables them to build a workforce to go into these areas and sensitively ask about living circumstances and collect vital Census data from people living in improvised dwellings and having a rough go of things."

The 122,494 people estimated to be experiencing homelessness on Census Night in 2021 represented a 5.2 per cent increase on the 2016 survey.

"People can be homeless and working full-time jobs, in full-time education, with children, living next door to us," Dr Allen said.

The previous Census occurred during the COVID pandemic when there was deliberate government policy to house those sleeping rough to reduce infection risk.

"I do expect that we will see a change in the proportion of people doing it tough; it's likely to increase," Dr Allen said.

Al-Hassan family members Rafkar, Tileva, Bahin, Hassan and Akito complete their Census online together. (ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds)

Census important for minority groups

In refugee households like the Al-Hassan family, often the children lead in answering census questions.

Bahin Al-Hassan, 16, was among local multicultural volunteers producing community language videos about the Census in the language he calls Ezidi, also known as Yazidi or Yezidi.

Bahin Al-Hassan has created videos about the Census for his community. (ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds)

"The Census has been a very important thing to our community and they are trying to get recognised as a region, a religion, as well as a language," he said.

The Ezidi community gathered in several refugee settlement regional cities this week for Roja Resh, a day of mourning for ISIS attacks in Iraq and Syria, which led to the death and enslavement of thousands of Ezidi people, and the displacement of hundreds of thousands more.

Coffs Harbour's Yezidi community gathered this week for Rojah Resh, a commemoration event of the 2014 genocide by ISIS fighters. (ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds)

The Census reports on the faith as Yezidi, but outside of the top nine religions, individuals must tick the "other" box and write in the field provided.

Coffs Harbour community leader Sami Sheebo has been campaigning for the community he calls Yazidi to be listed as its own check box, seeing it as an important step towards visibility for the community.

"Basically, we want to recognise [the] Yazidi community. So, we want to be recognised as Yazidi," she said.

" We will keep advocating, educating people and try to prove to the Australian government how many Yazidi people there are, through this Census. "

Sami Sheebo wants Yezidi listed in ethnicity, language and religion Census questions. (ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds)

Australia's Yezidi population grew from 63 people in 2016 to 4,123 in the 2021 Census.

The Jewish community is another community pushing for the same recognition.

Executive Council of Australian Jewry (ECAJ) co-chief executive Peter Wertheim estimates there are 117,000 Jewish people in Australia, although the Census set the population at 99,956.

"The tick box answers to the religion question have never included the numerically smaller faith communities, like the Jewish community," Mr Wertheim said.

Peter Wertheim says historical misuse of Census data overseas causes mistrust. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

Mr Wertheim said rising antisemitism had impacted the confidence of Jewish people in recording their faith.

"It's heightened the sense of exclusion, but it has also heightened the traditional concerns of confidentiality and data protection of Census data," he said.

"Any Jewish family can tell you of experiences in previous times when totalitarian regimes have used censuses to make lists of Jewish people, who are then targeted for persecution or even worse."

Census night is on Tuesday.

World.title: From Chicken Fried to Kiwi sledge: How Aussies won historic Olympic gold
World.content:
Shannon Parry was on a morning jog in Brisbane a few years back when she was stopped in her tracks.

Running past a primary school, she noticed a group of girls, aged no more than eight years old, playing rugby.

As the co-captain of Australia's victorious women's rugby sevens team at the 2016 Olympics, Parry was struck by the sight.

Parry didn't start playing rugby until she was 18 because the opportunities to do so weren't as readily available when she was younger.

To see primary school-aged girls tossing the ball around had a profound impact on Parry, as the significance of what she and her teammates achieved at the Rio Olympics hit home.

"I was like, 'Wow,'" Parry tells ABC Sport.

"These girls have this opportunity partly because of what we've been able to create around the legacy of Rio.

"For me, it was special."

Shannon Parry (right) was Australia's co-captain at the Rio Olympics. (Getty Images/World Rugby: Dan Mullan)

August 8 marks the 10th anniversary of Australia's historic triumph in Rio, which was the first time rugby sevens was contested at an Olympics.

A victory for women's sport Shannon Parry hails Australia's Olympic gold medal in rugby sevens as not only a victory for the nation but also women's sport.

It's difficult to measure its legacy as this continues to be felt.

For some current Australian players in the sevens and Wallaroos programs, Australia's Rio gold medal inspired them to play rugby.

Australian sevens co-captain Bella Nasser told ABC Sport earlier this year she'd "never looked at rugby as a female sport until that moment".

Wallaroos star Piper Duck was similarly motivated to take up the game, having previously thought "women weren't allowed to play".

Australia's Rio victory inspired many girls to take up rugby. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Parry is humbled to learn the likes of Nasser and Duck look to Australia's 2016 team as trailblazers.

"The players coming through now have idols they can look up to," Parry says.

"To think that 2016 team had a small impact on getting those girls and encouraging them to try rugby, it's pretty special."

Developing a world-class program

Australia's Rio victory didn't come by chance.

It was the culmination of Rugby Australia's (RA) astute planning, which began as early as 2012 when the governing body, then known as the Australian Rugby Union, hosted talent identification camps.

Several members of the Rio gold medal-winning squad joined the sevens program following these camps, coming from sports such as rugby league, touch football, athletics and basketball.

Less than four years out from the Rio Olympics, some had never picked up a rugby ball until this time.

Another crucial step towards winning the Olympic gold was RA's decision to centralise the program in Sydney at the beginning of 2014.

Based at the Sydney Academy of Sport and Recreation in the Northern Beaches suburb of Narrabeen, 21 players took up full-time contracts.

The Australian squad pictured at its Sydney training base. (Reuters: David Gray)

Parry had played for both the Australian sevens team and Wallaroos by this stage but was also holding down a job.

Accepting a one-year deal with virtually no guarantees was a massive leap of faith.

"It was a bit of a shock to most of us, to be honest, because a lot of us were working full-time," says Parry, who first played for Australia in sevens in 2013.

"I was a full-time teacher, and we were just juggling rugby on the side.

"We had a camp down at Bond University just before Christmas in 2013 and they [RA] said, 'We're going to go full-time. Here's a contract and meet us in Sydney at this address and we're going to embark on this journey.'

"We were like, 'OK.'"

Shannon Parry (right) played for both the Australian sevens team and Wallaroos. (Reuters: David Rowland)

Parry was one of only a few players on the full-time contract list who had a background in rugby before playing sevens.

Among those fresh to the game was Emilee Barton (nee Cherry).

As a child living in the south-west Queensland town of Roma, Barton dreamt of playing sport on the international stage.

"Growing up, I played every sport under the sun and loved it," Barton says.

Barton was a touch football star until rugby entered her orbit in 2012, the same year she made her Australian sevens debut.

Emilee Barton became one of the key players in the Australian squad. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Becoming a full-time rugby player helped Barton's career blossom, as she was named the International Rugby Board's (now World Rugby) Women's Sevens Player of the Year in 2014.

"It was empowering to be invested in by Rugby Australia," Barton says.

"For them to say, 'We think this can be a world-class program, we think you can win a gold medal at the Olympic Games' gave a real sense of ownership to our playing group.

"We wanted to show them we did have the ability and work ethic to create a program from the ground up."

Prior to the establishment of a full-time sevens program, RA made another important call.

Appointing Tim Walsh as head coach in late 2013 would prove to be a master stroke.

'Shift of power'

Walsh had played professionally in 15-a-side rugby and represented Australia in sevens before moving into the coaching ranks.

His will to win was evident early in his playing career.

As Australia's fullback in an under-19 international against New Zealand in 1988, Walsh slotted a field goal from 48 metres out, with just seconds left on the clock, to clinch a 25-23 triumph.

Tim Walsh represented Australia in rugby sevens. (Getty Images: Christopher Lee)

It therefore came as little surprise when Walsh declared he wanted the Australian women's sevens team to achieve "dominance and success" after he took charge of the program in September 2013.

The task at hand was going to be challenging, however, as the Australians had finished fifth in the inaugural 2012/13 Women's Sevens World Series.

They then exited the 2013 Rugby World Cup Sevens at the quarterfinal stage following a 14-10 defeat to Spain.

In both competitions, New Zealand emerged triumphant.

"Back then, ours was a bit of a nothing program," Barton admits.

Tim Walsh made a winning debut as Australia's coach. (Getty Images: Mark Evans)

But progress was made in the 2013/14 World Series, with Australia marking Walsh's debut as coach with a 35-27 upset win over New Zealand in the final of the opening tournament in Dubai.

Interestingly, eight members of Australia's 12-player squad in Dubai would appear at the Rio Olympics, with Parry and Barton among them.

"That early win gave us confidence," Walsh says.

Another win in São Paulo and two runner-up placings in Guangzhou and Amsterdam saw Australia finish second to New Zealand in the World Series standings.

Australia pictured during the Guangzhou World Series tournament in 2014. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

New Zealand remained the pacesetter the following season but during the penultimate leg of the 2014/15 World Series in London, Walsh could tell Australia was on the right track.

His squad recorded a 24-5 win over their trans-Tasman counterparts in the semis, followed by a 20-17 defeat of Canada in the final.

Australia's victory in London was a turning point for the program. (Getty Images: Tony Marshall)

Australia would eventually finish third behind New Zealand and Canada on the World Series standings, but its rivals had been put on notice.

"The momentum shift happened in 2015," Walsh says.

"We beat New Zealand in the London semifinal. We played really well. Chloe Dalton nailed this kick from the sideline.

"Every attribute of our game was covered. We had kickers, we had re-start reception, we had speed, we had experience, we had ball players, we had X factor.

"That [London] was the shift. From then, we pretty much were the best team from that moment.

"It was the shift of power."

The team to beat

By the time the 2015/16 World Series rolled around, Australia's decision to go full time with its women's sevens program had been vindicated.

The squad had embraced professionalism and developed a ruthless attitude, which was reflected in the improved results.

"From the outset, some of them were school teachers, radiographers, full-time workers," Walsh says.

"They gave up their careers to move to Sydney and be paid peanuts to chase a dream, so they had that commitment.

"The ones who didn't do it were weeded out.
