"So you ended up with the best of the best, who had the absolute purpose and focus to go on and achieve something special."

Parry adds: "Day in, day out it was about winning a gold medal."

Australia poses with the 2015/16 World Series trophy. (AP: Rick Rycroft)

With the Rio Olympics on the horizon, Australia won the 2015/16 World Series on the back of three victories from five tournaments.

Adding to Australia's growing self-belief was the fact it was undefeated against New Zealand, which would finish second on the standings.

"The team, in that final year, had this belief and we're in that state of flow that all coaches and teams are looking for," Walsh says.

"There was nothing that was going to stop them."

Even a loss to Canada in the final of the concluding World Series leg in France was regarded as nothing more than a hiccup.

"We beat the Kiwis in the semis [14-5] and we came into the final and Canada actually beat us 29-19," Parry says.

"For us it was a case of, 'Oh, that's right, we've got to turn up and play our best every game.'

"It wasn't a reality check, but we knew we've got to be able to turn it on when we need to be able to."

Ellia Green starred for Australia during the triumphant 2015/2016 campaign. (Getty Images: Warren Little)

By virtue of its World Series victory, Australia was installed as the gold medal favourite in Rio.

Such a mantle comes with pressure and expectation, but Australia was undaunted.

"We didn't talk about it [favouritism] much," Barton says.

"We wanted to go into Rio being incredibly humble and painting the narrative that the Kiwis were heavy favourites as well, especially with a much more experienced team than what we had.

"We obviously did analysis on other teams, but it was always looking at ourselves internally and worrying about what we could do."

Favouritism sat comfortably with Walsh.

"We addressed that, going in as number one and favourites, and we owned it," he says.

Olympic campaign begins

The Olympic competition wasn't the first time the Australian squad had been to Rio.

Australia's 2016 Olympic squad Shannon Parry (co-captain) Sharni Smale (nee Williams, co-captain) Nicole Beck Emilee Barton (nee Cherry) Chloe Dalton Gemma Etheridge Ellia Green Evania Isaako (nee Pelite) Alicia Lucas (nee Quirk) Emma Verran (nee Tonegato) Amy Turner Charlotte Caslick

In 2015, Walsh and his players visited the site where rugby sevens would make its Games debut.

The temporary grandstands at what would become known as Deodoro Stadium hadn't been erected, but the players got the chance to experience the surrounds well in advance of the Olympics.

"Walshy has his ways of getting people visualising," says Parry, who would share the captaincy with Sharni Smale [nee Williams] in Rio.

"So we all took our shoes off and lay on the ground and looked at the sky.

"He said, 'We're going to win the Olympic gold medal here.'"

Fast forward to the Games themselves, and Australia found itself alongside Fiji, United States and Colombia in Group A.

Dominant wins over Colombia (53-0) and Fiji (36-0) meant Australia secured top spot in the group ahead of its final match against the US, which ended in a 12-12 draw.

The clash with the Americans had no bearing on Australia's passage to the quarterfinals but it provided the backdrop to an iconic moment.

Charlotte Caslick's breathtaking cover tackle on a flying Victoria Folayan would be remembered for years to come.

"You could see this fluorescent yellow jersey come across the field and it was Charlotte," Walsh recalls.

"Sixty kilos, running like the Terminator, and then she just absolutely belted her [Folayan] with a textbook tackle.

"She jumped to her feet, before Victoria even took a breath, and looked down and gave her a look of, 'Gotcha.'

Charlotte Caslick's tackle on Victoria Folayan became an iconic moment. (Getty Images/World Rugby: Dan Mullan)

"She then flicked a ponytail over the back of her head and walked off.

"I just remember vividly being on the sideline looking at that and going, 'Oh my God.'

"It just changed the perception of rugby forever."

Caslick would figure prominently in the knockout stages, with Australia comfortably advancing to the final.

Light work was made of Spain in the quarterfinals via a 24-0 win, before Canada was swept aside 17-5 in the semis.

Ellia Green (left) was among Australia's try scorers in the quarterfinal win over Spain. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

Meanwhile, New Zealand, unbeaten in group play, progressed to the gold medal match following victories over the US (5-0) and Great Britain (25-7).

Having failed to defeat Australia since February 2015, New Zealand wasn't expected to be in an antagonising mood as it prepared for the final.

New Zealand coach Sean Horan had other ideas.

'Extra motivation'

Following the semifinal win over Great Britain, Horan was interviewed on New Zealand TV.

When asked about facing Australia in the final, he questioned the toughness of the World Series champions.

"The Australians don't like pressure, they don't like the physical side,' Horan proclaimed.

New Zealand coach Sean Horan provided Australia with additional motivation. (Getty Images: Chris Graythen)

The comment didn't go unnoticed among Australian reporters at Deodoro Stadium, while it quickly lit up social media.

Nor did it escape the attention of Walsh.

"We wrote it up on the board," Walsh says with a wry chuckle.

"We did use that as some extra motivation."

While digesting Horan's taunt was a late addition to Australia's preparations, there was a ritual the players always observed moments before running onto the field.

"Our song for the campaign was Chicken Fried, by Zac Brown Band," Parry explains.

"That was sort of our gee-up song to get us ready. It was the song we played the whole year.

"Whenever that song came on it was time to go, time for action."

But a delay to the start of the final meant there was time for the song to be played more than usual.

"We were like, 'OK, just play the song again,' so we played it again," Parry says.

"Our strength and conditioning coach Craig Twentyman was banging on the demountable walls inside the dressing room and they were shaking.

"It was literally like we were having a rave in there. People would have been saying, 'What is going on in there?'

"Everyone was singing and dancing. The physio and doctor were in there. It was going off.

"We were having our own little rave before going out. It was crazy."

Australia was in a relaxed state once it took the field for the final. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

Walsh fondly remembers the moment, as passers-by mistakenly thought the Australians were celebrating.

"The team was dancing around, and the lights were flicking on and off," Walsh says.

"A couple of [Olympic] volunteers and logistical staff were walking past and knocked on the door and said, 'Congratulations, great work.'

"We replied, 'We haven't even played yet.'

"It was a unique way of preparing for a brutal sport."

Tight first half

Relaxed, yet focused, Australia ran onto the pitch alongside New Zealand, knowing history was about to be made.

As a healthy gathering of Australian and New Zealand fans watched from the stands under the Rio night sky, Parry and her teammates received the kick-off but found themselves trailing on the scoreboard midway through the first half.

A crooked line-out throw 5 metres from Australia's goal line gave New Zealand possession, which it converted into points through Kayla McAlister's opening try on the left edge.

"They got the hop on us early," Parry says.

"That got rid of any nervousness and we said to each other, 'OK, now it's time to play footy.'"

Emma Verran scored Australia's first try in the final. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

Play footy they did, with the Australians levelling scores when Emma Verran (nee Tonegato) touched down in the right corner.

New Zealand supporters would later dispute the legitimacy of Verran's grounding of the ball, but referee Alhambra Nievas and in-goal judge Sakurako Kawasaki awarded the try.

It appeared the 5-5 scoreline would remain through to half-time, but an infringement from New Zealand great Portia Woodman-Wickliffe (nee Woodman) inside the final 10 seconds of the term gave Australia another opportunity.

Evania Isaako's try put Australia ahead 10-5 at half-time. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Woodman-Wickliffe was shown a yellow card, leaving New Zealand with just six players for two minutes.

Australia capitalised on the numerical advantage by creating an overlap for Evania Isaako (nee Pelite) to cross for a try out wide and establish a 10-5 lead at the break.

"I vividly remember what Walshy said at half-time," Parry remembers.

"He said, 'Look over there. There's a gold medal hanging off that crossbar. You've just got to get it.'"

'We're not losing this'

Defending a five-point lead, Barton was confident Australia's superior conditioning would shine through in the second half.

"I think one of our strengths was our fitness and being able to compete for the whole game," Barton says.

Walsh knew Australia had the psychological edge, having noted the "steely" look in the eyes of the players.

"I was like, 'We're not losing this,'" he says.

Australia's Alicia Lucas (right) tackles New Zealand opponent Gayle Broughton. (AP: Zsolt Czegledi)

Australia carried its momentum into the second half and appeared to put the result beyond doubt with back-to-back tries scored by Ellia Green and Caslick.

Both were converted by Chloe Dalton and with less than 4 minutes to play, Australia held a commanding 24-5 lead.

New Zealand cut the margin back through McAlister's second try, but it was a case of too little, too late.

With the full-time siren having already sounded, Woodman-Wickliffe dotted down under the posts for another consolation try, leaving Australia to rejoice following a 24-17 victory.

Australia celebrated once the full-time whistle had rung out. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

"I'd come off the field with maybe 3 minutes to go," Parry says.

"I remember when there was 2 minutes to go, it felt like the longest 2 minutes standing on the sideline.

Aussies win sevens gold in Rio Australia creates history with a 24-17 victory over New Zealand in the first Olympic rugby sevens final.

"It was then literally 30 seconds, 20 seconds, and it was like, 'Oh my God, we've won this. This is unbelievable.'

"We were just so ecstatic. Everything had come down to that one game, really.

"Two and a half years of footy for one game."

Walsh wasn't prepared to celebrate until referee Nievas had blown the full-time whistle.

"I think there were 10 seconds on the clock and [Australia manager] Scotty Bowen was next to me," Walsh says.

"He was like, 'Mate, we've done it,' and I said, 'No we haven't. Wait until the whistle goes. Something could happen.'"

New Zealand felt the emotional pain of defeat at full-time. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Even the most diehard Australian supporter couldn't help but feel for the New Zealand players, who were inconsolable.

The sight of a collapsed Woodman-Wickliffe sobbing on the ground remains an enduring memory.

Emilee Barton (centre) enjoys the spoils of victory with Alicia Lucas (left) and Ellia Green. (Reuters: Geoff Burke)

Given the rivalry between the two nations, Barton feels it was fitting they shared the historic moment.

"I guess it was poetic to meet them in the first Olympic final," Barton says.

"To win it was incredible."

The Rio legacy

Walsh admits he gets "goosebumps" when reflecting on the impact Australia's win in Rio had on women's rugby.

Not only did the gold medal spark massive growth in participation numbers in sevens and 15-a-side rugby, but it also helped changed the perception of women's contact sports.

"One thing that really stuck with me at the time was my first son was three or four years old," Walsh says.

"We were walking through Bondi Junction where there was a store with all these TVs.

"I stopped and was watching a rugby league game and my son asked, 'Are you watching the girls play?' and I said, 'No, I'm watching the boys.'

"He looked at me and said, 'Do boys play rugby too?'

"It was a real light-bulb moment."

Australia is the current world champion in women's sevens. (Reuters: Catherine Steenkeste)

Walsh remains a key figure in women's rugby, having recently coached Australia to the sevens World Championship in the concluding act of his second stint in the role.

He began working as RA's director of women's high-performance last month, a position in which he will oversee the alignment of the sevens and Wallaroos programs.

Barton retired in 2021 after a glittering career featuring 131 World Series tries.

She joined Walsh's coaching staff the following year and was inducted into World Rugby's Hall of Fame in 2024.

Shannon Parry went on to play in the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. (Instagram: Shannon Parry)

Parry, who retired from sevens in 2021 and 15-a-side rugby two years later, remains heavily invested in the sport.

She is Queensland Sevens head coach and worked on the Reds' staff for their 2026 Super Rugby Women's campaign.

Parry's involvement with the game means she sees the impact of Australia's Rio victory up close.

Whether it be primary school-aged girls getting the chance to play rugby for the first time or inspiring women to embark on professional careers in the game, its significance will never diminish.

"When I first put the Aussie jersey on, I remember saying to myself if I can encourage one girl to play rugby that's a win," Parry says.

"You look at the pathways and grassroots now and the opportunities young girls get, it's fantastic and great to see.

"I think a lot of people look back to that runway in 2016 where it started the trajectory of not only girls' rugby, but girls' sport and giving it the light it deserves."

World.title: New US ambassador to Australia finally gets the nod to head to Canberra
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations New US ambassador to Australia finally gets the nod to head to Canberra Michael Koziol Updated August 8, 2026 — 7:12am ,first published 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The US Senate has confirmed former Republican congressman David Brat to become ambassador to Australia, clearing the way for him to fill the diplomatic post that has sat empty for nearly two years. Brat was part of a block of 74 nominations, including judicial and diplomatic postings, approved on Friday afternoon (US time) ahead of the long summer recess. Trump nominated him for the role in April. Nominated US ambassador to Australia David Brat during his confirmation hearing at the US Senate in May. US Congress It means he can arrive in Canberra ahead of the 75th anniversary of the ANZUS treaty between Australia, New Zealand and the US, which will be commemorated on September 1. In the US, Brat is best known as the Tea Party insurgent who ousted sitting House of Representatives speaker Eric Cantor in a Republican primary in 2014, before the rise of Trump.



Related Article Opinion

Steve Bannon Trump will declare a ‘national emergency’ before midterms: Bannon Peter Hartcher Political and international editor The New York Times called it “one of the most stunning primary election upsets in congressional history”. Cantor had been a seven-term congressman, and Brat beat him on the right with a focus on immigration. He lost the Virginia seat to Democrat Abigail Spanberger in 2018, and returned to academia, becoming senior vice president of business relations at a private evangelical college, Liberty University. Brat has also been a regular guest and fill-in host on Steve Bannon’s influential MAGA podcast War Room. In one of his most recent appearances, in January, he defended the actions of federal agents in Minnesota who were at that time being criticised over the death of US citizen Renee Good.



“The Washington Post or The New York Times, if anyone went into their office and started throwing bottles at them, lighting up bottle rockets, hitting people, threatening, spitting in their face, they’d be in their pillow rooms crying,” Brat said. “That’s what’s going on here. Our officers of law, our federal officers, are being assaulted on a daily basis.” David Brat pictured with Donald Trump in 2015. Getty Images Bannon told this masthead last month that he helped find Brat for the Republicans back in 2014 - and that the former congressman would be “the perfect man for the job” in Canberra. “David was a forerunner of populist nationalism, he has access to the highest levels of power and he has a big presence in MAGA media,” Bannon said.



Brat, 62, was born in Detroit and gained a bachelor of arts from Michigan’s Hope College, before obtaining his masters in divinity at Princeton Theological Seminary, and a PhD. He is also an economist who was once described as a “free-market purist”. But recently, he has defended Trump’s tariffs, arguing they were aimed at addressing unfair trade practices. As ambassador, Brat will have to navigate key matters in the US-Australia alliance including the AUKUS defence pact, critical minerals and Australia’s treatment of the America-dominated tech industry. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Money, drugs and affection used to lure children into crime
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaChild safety Money, drugs and affection used to lure children into crime Angus Delaney August 8, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Children in state care are being recruited by criminals into offending, setting them on a course through the justice system that can leave them with long-lasting psychological trauma. An inquiry by the Victorian Commission for Children and Young People into the experiences of under-14s in the justice system found residential care is a recruiting ground for criminals who ply vulnerable kids with money, drugs and cynical affection. Commissioner for Children and Young People Tracy Beaton said children in residential care were vulnerable to exploitation. Alex Coppel Children told the commission that residential care – which houses Victoria’s children who cannot safely live with their families or find a place in foster care – conditioned them to crime and “gets you used to jail”. The commission’s With us, not against us inquiry, tabled to parliament last week, examined the lives of 26 children aged under 14 who passed through the justice system between 2023 and 2025.



It urged the government to raise the age of criminal responsibility from 12 to 14 and devote greater resources to early-intervention programs. It also cautioned against punitive custodial sentences for children. However, it comes at a time when both state political parties are announcing crime crackdowns and children are overrepresented in violent crime statistics. In the year to March 2026, they made up more than 60 per cent of robberies, and about half of all carjackings and home invasions. Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush has said that many young offenders are “focused on impressing their mates and have no idea of the consequences of their offending on the victims, themselves, their families and the community”. Tracy Beaton, the state’s Commissioner for Children and Young People, said children in residential care were highly vulnerable and often exploited.



“It is actually really important that you look to see how you can best decriminalise behaviour of children ... and give them hope, and actually hold adults to account for children,” Beaton told The Age. Archer, a 25-year-old who previously lived in residential care, told the inquiry he was exposed to “proper criminals” who know how to manipulate vulnerable children. An inquiry by the Victorian Commission for Children and Young People found residential care is a recruiting ground for criminals who ply vulnerable kids with money, drugs and cynical affection. Getty Images “They know how to talk, how to convince you,” he said. “They make it sound easy and safe. They influence your decisions without you realising it.” Chris, a 16-year-old and former occupant, told the commission that children in residential care were sometimes forced to commit crimes by adults who got them addicted to drugs or money. “A lot of stuff gets blamed on kids now, but a lot of the time it’s adults,” he said.



A spokesperson for the government said it had made significant investments in child protection, including by creating access to therapeutic supports for all young people in residential care. Related Article Exclusive

Crime ‘Parasites’: How organised crime is feeding off the youth gang crisis “It is important to recognise that residential care provides a home where children live and is not a custodial setting,” the spokesperson said. “As is appropriate, children in care should be free to engage in social and community activities outside of the home, in the same manner as their peers.” Victoria has the lowest use of residential care nationally. The inquiry found current practice is failing to rehabilitate young offenders and said it was limited because Labor had not publicly released a report the government commissioned almost three years ago into keeping young Victorians out of the justice system.



The commission’s report was tabled four months before a state election where both major parties are burnishing their tough-on-crime credentials. In his first speech as premier, Ben Carroll said crimes committed under his government would be “dealt with to meet the community’s expectations”. Then-premier Jacinta Allan backflipped on her promise to raise the age of criminal responsibility to 14 after a series of high-profile and violent youth crimes. Allan also introduced “adult time for violent crime” laws that remove the assumption of bail for juvenile offenders and allow courts to treat children as young as 14 charged with select violent crimes as adult offenders. In his first press conference as premier, Ben Carroll indicated community safety would be a priority for his government. Jason South Shadow attorney-general James Newbury last week said the Coalition, if it wins the state election, would add theft of a motor vehicle, attempted carjacking and reckless conduct endangering life to the laws. “We’re going to get tougher on crime, tougher on youth offenders,” Newbury said.



Beaton said research showed longer, harsher sentences on child offenders did not reduce crime and the community would be safer if a more rehabilitative approach was taken. She said whichever party was in government, she hoped they made evidence-based policies. Related Article Courts Teen offenders in city’s ‘bar wars’ coached on how to minimise crimes: police “It feels really tricky when people say, we should be tough on crime,” she said. “We are not saying that you shouldn’t ask children to wear the consequence of their behaviour, we’re just saying that there’s a different way of doing that.” Commissioner for Aboriginal Children and Young People Dallas Widdicombe said children who entered the justice system before the age of 14 overwhelmingly came from disadvantaged backgrounds and had histories of family violence, poverty and homelessness. “[They] have not been able to be children,” he said.



Youth mentor Lueth Akue, who worked on the inquiry and serves on the commission in an advisory role, spent time in custody when he was 16. His family fled a war-torn country, but their trauma followed them to Melbourne. His mother coped through substance abuse, and his father walked out when he was 10. Poverty, homelessness, racism, family violence and a lack of intervention or support saw Akue enter the justice system. It was only after he hit “crisis point” that support became available. Akue worked closely with a case worker and developed a strong support network which allowed him to turn his life around. Akue, now aged 26, said the psychological impact of going through the justice system as a child was still with him. “It’s hard for you to step back into pro-social groups ... because you feel different: you feel like you don’t belong,” he said. “It’s much easier for you to go back to where you feel like you belong, which is in a negative social group.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Trump takes ballroom to Supreme Court after judges order stop to construction
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump takes ballroom to Supreme Court after judges order stop to construction Michael Koziol August 8, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Two judges have ordered Donald Trump to cease construction of his beloved White House ballroom in a blistering rebuke of the president’s actions that sets up a showdown in the Supreme Court. The Court of Appeals in Washington ruled on Friday (US time) that Trump must obtain approval from the US Congress for his ballroom plans, though it agreed that construction of underground bunkers and military facilities could continue. Construction of the White House ballroom, on the right, as well as a new helipad outside the residence, on the left. AP Photo/Allison Robbert The two majority judges sided with the National Trust for Historic Preservation, a conservation group which brought the lawsuit, and were blunt in their assessment. “We are aware of no instance in American history in which a president unilaterally and using privately collected funds demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorised to be built and American taxpayers paid for. Until now,” they wrote.



“At this preliminary stage, the National Trust has shown, compellingly, that Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the executive branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House – the People’s House – to fit a particular president’s desires.” A Trump-appointed judge, Neomi Rao, dissented from the majority ruling and said that the Trust had no standing to bring the legal challenge in the first place. US President Donald Trump, in May, showing reporters the latest plans for his ballroom. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin She said the ballroom likely sat within the president’s authority to make improvements to the executive residence at the White House, and aesthetic objections to it were of low importance. The lower court had “elevated the aesthetic displeasure of a single passerby over the government’s security interests in the ballroom and the security risks of leaving an open construction site at the President’s home and office”, Rao wrote.



The Trust’s case was brought on behalf of Alison Hoagland, an architectural historian and local Washington resident who alleged that the ballroom would disturb her walks through the city. Rao said Hoagland did not have legal standing to sue – that she is not affected by the ballroom – a position Trump has himself taken. A render of Trump’s proposed White House ballroom shown to the Commission of Fine Arts on February 19. The president said on Friday (Saturday AEST) that he would immediately appeal the “horrendous, politically motivated and unlawful ruling” to the Supreme Court. In a 500-word post on Truth Social, Trump entwined the underground military components of the project – which the court said could continue – with the above-ground ballroom.



“Two Obama and Biden Appellate Court Judges just voted against the desperately needed Military Centre, required for the National Security of Washington DC and our Country itself,” he said. Related Article Updated

Trump's White House ‘Don’t ever talk again’: Trump loses his cool over Reflecting Pool fiasco “The Circuit Court’s decision … severely jeopardises the lives and welfare of the people who work, and will be working, at the White House – including all future Presidents of the United States and their families.” Trump is likely to regard the Supreme Court appeal as a test of several judges’ loyalty. He has lashed out at the court – which has a 6-3 conservative majority – since it struck down his so-called reciprocal tariffs and an executive order on birthright citizenship. Amy Coney Barrett, whom Trump appointed to the court after the death of Ruth Bader Ginsburg in his first term, found against him on both matters.





Trump is also building a new helipad on the South Lawn of the White House, just outside the main residence. And he is advancing plans for a “Triumphal Arch” to be built near Arlington Cemetery. The ballroom itself is only expected to be completed near the end of Trump’s term, in 2028. He has argued it is a necessary addition for future presidents to hold large functions such as state dinners that have, in the past, been held in makeshift tents on the White House lawn. World.title: The simple $174,000 question many retirees still get wrong
World.content:
August 8, 2026 — 5:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I got asked a simple question on social media this week, one that most people in the retirement and superannuation industry think people already know the answer to. But to my surprise, it sparked an enormous conversation. The question was “If I’m retired why wouldn’t I just take all my money out of super and put it in the bank?” Apparently, many people are unaware of the benefits of keeping their money in super, and don’t know about the really juicy upside of moving your superannuation into a retirement phase account so you can enjoy tax-free income when you’re retired. So today we’re going back to basics – to what actually happens to your money the day you retire and why that decision, more than almost any other that you’ll make determines how far your retirement savings might stretch. A question of super. Simon Letch While you’re working, your super sits in what’s called the accumulation phase. Most people reach retirement today with a reasonable or even large balance in their accumulation phase account, unable to access it until they meet two key conditions: reaching the official superannuation access age of 60, and ceasing just one job/employment relationship (even if they go back to work elsewhere afterwards) or, or simply turning 65 at which point you can access your super unconditionally, whether you’re working or not.



During your working phase of your life, you contribute to your superannuation account chiefly from your employer contributions, which are taxed at up to 15 per cent on the way in up to the concessional contribution cap of $32,500. And once the money is inside super investment earnings are taxed at 15 per cent and capital gains at up to 10 per cent because superannuation still gets a one-third discount on assets held longer than 12 months. Why on earth does the bank feel more compelling? I think it comes down to familiarity. But from the day you retire you’re allowed to move some or all of that money, up to $2.1 million, into a retirement phase account, sometimes labelled a retirement pension, account-based pension or income stream, depending on your fund. And the minute your money lands in this account, you benefit because the earnings on that money becomes completely tax-free. There’s no income tax payable and no tax on the capital gains. And moreover, you can draw money out at any time either as a lump sum or as a regular income stream that can feel much like a pay cheque, though funds do require you to draw down a minimum amount each year, once you’re in the retirement phase, starting at 4 per cent of your balance if you’re under 65, and rising as you get older.



That means every single dollar your investments earn inside your retirement account is yours to keep, and if your investments are growing, you can let them compound even more strongly than they might have in an accumulation account where the taxman would take 15 per cent out in tax on earnings each year. Editor's pick Opinion

Home loans Why your bank might be overcharging you interest – and how to check Bec Wilson Money contributor When you move your money from an accumulation account into a retirement account, it stays invested – and you still have choices around how it’s invested and how much risk you want exposure to. But if you stayed invested in the same things, and just switched accounts, the returns for the retirement phase would be higher, simply because of the tax. Now compare that to the bank account that my community member was tempted by. Every dollar of interest you earn from a bank account gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your full marginal rate. If you’ve still got a part-time wage coming in or any other income sources kicking along outside super that could mean handing 30, 37 or even 45¢ in every dollar to the tax office. Inside a retirement account, that growth will cost you nothing.



Let’s compare the latest returns on superannuation funds in both the accumulation and retirement phase, which Chant West released just over a week ago, with how someone who’d put all their retirement savings into a bank account. Chant West’s own data shows exactly what that tax difference is worth to someone’s hip pocket. Take the Hostplus Balanced fund. Held in an ordinary accumulation phase account it returned 8.9 per cent a year over the 10 years to June 2026. Held in the retirement phase, the same investment strategy, same fund, same underlying assets returned 10.1 per cent a year. That’s a gap of more than a full percentage point every single year purely because of tax. Compound that over a 25 or 30 year retirement, and it’s the difference between having enough or rationing your money carefully to make it through the last decade. To bring this picture to life, I asked Chant West’s Ian Fryer to run the numbers for someone retiring at 65 with $500,000 in their super, drawing the minimum required 5 per cent a year for the next 10 years, using the returns from mid-2016 to mid-2026.



If that $500,000 had gone into term deposits instead, drawing the same 5 per cent out every single year, the retiree would have ended their decade with about $404,000. On the surface that looks OK, but once you strip out the inflation rate, that $404,000 is really only worth about $299,000. In real terms their savings had gone backwards by more than a third. Now, let’s compare that with the same $500,000 left in a typical balanced retirement account inside super, invested with around half in growth assets and drawing the same 5 per cent a year. Based purely on that those funds were targeted to earn, which is usually CPI + 2.75 per cent, they’d already have finished the decade ahead, at around $521,000. And because balanced super funds have actually beaten their own targets over the last 10 years, the real-world median returns leaves that retiree, 10 years later, with $579,000, which is worth about $427,000 once you adjust for inflation. Stop and think about it. That’s the same starting balance, and the same amount drawn from super every year for 10 years. The only thing that changed was where the money sat – either in a term deposit at the bank or inside a retirement phase superannuation account. The gap between the two is $174,000 in nominal terms, or roughly $129,000 once you account for inflation. That’s tax-free compounding in action.



Editor's pick Opinion

Home loans Three steps to protect your home loan from a falling market Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor So why on earth does the bank feel more compelling? I think it comes down to familiarity. People understand bank accounts and term deposits - they’ve had them their whole life. They can log in, see their money sitting there and sleep at night without the markets moving around while they sleep. Super, by comparison can feel like a bit of a black box, run by someone you don’t know as well, invested in things you’ve never really understood. And the balance can move around in ways that make you uncomfortable. And then there’s the fear of the government tinkering with it, something that is increasingly coming to the fore in every education session I run. If you feel that way, you’re clearly not alone – thousands of people on Facebook felt the same this week. But there’s more to learn about super as you approach retirement because in the retirement phase it does something exceptional – it grows, completely tax-free. And that might be more valuable than you’d ever contemplated.



Bec Wilson is author of the bestseller How to Have an Epic Retirement and the newly released Prime Time: 27 Lessons for the New Midlife. She writes a weekly newsletter at epicretirement.net and hosts the Prime Time podcast. World.title: Three steps to protect your home loan from a falling market
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingHome loans Opinion Three steps to protect your home loan from a falling market Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor August 8, 2026 — 5:01am

August 8, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Directly after the federal budget on May 12, I began my column with the words: “Didn’t anybody drafting last week’s budget think of the 95 per cent first home buyers?” The budget – and its controversial tax changes – was ostensibly about helping younger Aussies onto the housing ladder by removing the artificial property inflators of negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount. It was meant to suppress the property market. Escalating interest rates have meant many are struggling to keep up with their mortgage repayments. Gabriele Charlotte The problem was that this was just after the government enticed a whole heap of first home buyers into the market… with just 5 per cent deposits. In my post-budget piece, I wrote: “In October last year, the government pulled the trigger – three months early – on a hugely expanded Home Guarantee Scheme, which allows first home buyers to purchase with a 5 per cent deposit and avoid expensive lenders’ mortgage insurance.”



This is usually payable below a 20 per cent deposit but, under the scheme, the government goes guarantor for 15 per cent of your property so you can avoid that insurance, which is often tens of thousands of dollars. But, as I wrote: “After paying your 5 per cent, leg-up-onto-the-ladder deposit, you take on a debt that is rungs and rungs higher than you otherwise might: 95 per cent.” Prices will, ultimately, start rising again. It’s just a matter of riding it out. And on October 1 last year, the allowable purchase price of the Home Guarantee Scheme was significantly lifted to include a bunch more properties and the means test abolished, to allow a bunch more first home buyers. In fact, all of them. Well, guess what? In the past week, debate has flared – in light of a smallish market retraction so far – about just how many newer home owners now owe more money than their property is worth.



The Coalition says tens of thousands of the 60,000-plus first home buyers who entered the market in that first six months (not all of whom used the scheme), are at risk of falling into negative equity, though the total number across all home owners remains under 1 per cent. Editor's pick Home loans This is how many home owners are actually in negative equity now So if you think you might be at risk, let’s get to the vital steps to avoiding negative equity stress. Firstly, where property prices will land remains to be seen. But it’s worth remembering that most existing investors will simply hold on – their perks are too good to give up and the blanket nature of the CGT rules (to the government’s credit) makes no competing investment more attractive (although super remains attractive). Underpinning property is that investors are far from panic selling. And that’s similar to what recent buyers need to avoid: being forced into pressure selling.



An asset’s value is only on paper; that value is only realised if you need to swap the asset for cold, hard cash. And the single key to avoiding that is being able to – ongoing – afford your repayments. That’s, of course, in the context of three rate rises so far this year. Pure and simple, it’s about your outgoings and your income. In the cost-of-living squeeze, recent home buyers in particular will have squeezed outgoings to the extreme – that’s part of what you have to do to qualify for a mortgage (especially a 95 per cent one!). But don’t miss either that to get a loan over the line, you must also pass a 300 basis-point interest-rate stress test. That means the lender has assessed that you can cope with 12 rate rises, where there have only been three. So, with the outgoings side of your life-ledger possibly sound, how secure is your income? Because losing this is the big risk you want to mitigate. Can you take steps to shore up your job? Do they recognise the contribution you are making? Perhaps you could even upskill to become more valuable to the business. The other employment unknown is illness or injury and there is insurance available for this: income protection.



Income protection is expensive but it is tax-deductible. You can also reduce its cost significantly by opting for a long wait period before it would begin to (75 per cent) replace your pay. And that’s where an emergency fund comes in. This can also subsidise you for the time until income protection insurance kicks in. Editor's pick Property prices End of the super-cycle: Big call on the national property market Indeed, the ideal is to have six months’ salary stashed – which may well be a pipe dream. But – for safety – just start squirrelling away what you can (for flexibility and access, the best place is in an offset account beside the mortgage in question). If it’s too late for all that though, know that your lender is required to have a dedicated hardship department that must extend you concessions if you get into financial strife. Instead of missing a repayment, as counterintuitive as it sounds, tell your lender you will struggle to make it beforehand. They’ll help – at least for a time.



Besides, missing a payment will affect your credit score. Entering a hardship arrangement with a lender will not; that arrangement will only be noted on your credit report, and not flow through to your score, for 12 months. The other thing to appreciate is that, even if you have found or do find yourself in negative equity, it should be brief. Prices will, ultimately, start rising again. It’s just a matter of riding it out. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. World.title: What happens when crime is no longer paying for our real estate?
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesResidential property What happens when crime is no longer paying for our real estate? Colin Kruger August 8, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Paying $15 million for a penthouse, even one with views of both the Sydney Harbour Bridge and Opera House from the outdoor hot tub, is feeling very 2025 as the slump in houses became a national phenomenon this week. Sydney and Melbourne are down more than 5 per cent from their peaks, according to property data group Cotality, while the property booms in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth are now deflating as well. The luxury penthouse was seized under proceeds of crime laws and was sold for millions less than its previous purchase price, despite a rising property market. But the buyers of the luxury penthouse in Sydney’s historic The Rocks district must have felt they got a bargain with its purchase last year, given the same property changed hands for $17.5 million in 2018. But the real winner appears to be the buyer of the sub-penthouse who picked it up for $9.4 million a few months later. It had changed hands for $14 million in 2019.



Both properties had been acquired at these questionably high prices by the same party, but the original owners had a lot more to grumble about than the multimillion dollar losses on the two transactions. In 2020, the two properties were put under a restraining order by the AFP-led Criminal Assets Confiscation Taskforce (CACT) - a team set up to confiscate the illegal wealth and assets of organised crime syndicates. Related Article Exclusive

Crime Underworld loses Sydney mansions, jewels, cars worth $1b in AFP raids CACT successfully seized the properties in 2024 as a result of Operation Cabestro, a Melbourne-based investigation into large-scale fraud involving imported alcohol which defrauded federal coffers of hundreds of millions of dollars. The multimillion-dollar losses on the sales appear to confirm that money launderers are not that picky about the price, as long as their ill-gotten gains get converted into respectable wealth - and potentially with a capital gain to boot.



To give an idea of how popular money is with our criminal class, since 2020, police have frozen about $1.2 billion in criminal assets. Two-thirds of that is related to property. Not any more. The criminal world’s free ride from rising property prices has been cruelled - as it has for the rest of us - via higher interest rates and changes to the tax treatment of capital gains. The tantalising question is, what additional downward pressure has there been on housing prices from the changes to anti-money laundering provisions last month which means tens of billions of dollars in criminal proceeds now have to find a new home? On July 1, real estate agents, accountants and lawyers came under Australia’s Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act for the first time. It means these parties will now have to know who their buyers and sellers are in any transaction and report any suspicious activity to police. A buyer can no longer just roll up to the selling agent with a boot load of cash and scant identification, no questions asked.



Australia’s financial crimes watchdog, AUSTRAC is in no doubt what impact this will have on house prices. AUSTRAC boss Brendan Thomas has said previously that it pushes up house prices and takes “property that would otherwise have been purchased by a hard-working Australian”. AUSTRAC CEO Brendan Thomas says criminal gangs are using professional enablers and shell companies to store illicit funds in the Australian real estate market. Max Mason-Hubers The Melbourne proceeds of crime that ended up in a Sydney penthouse will be much harder to carry out in this new environment, Thomas says. “We expect the reforms will bring more cases like this to light and help uncover money laundering in real estate transactions, that we don’t currently see, by bringing suspicious activity to our attention earlier,” he said.



But not everyone thinks it will have an impact on your average home price. “From a price perspective, we don’t expect a major impact - property values are still driven by supply, demand and interest rates,” Dr Nicola Powell, chief economist at real estate portal Domain, says. “What these reforms will do is lift transparency and add more rigour, particularly in higher-value or more complex transactions,” she says. AMP’s chief economist Shane Oliver says there doesn’t appear to be any reliable estimates of the value of money laundered through property, but it looks to be less than one per cent of transactions. He said it’s likely biased towards the upper end of the property market, which appears to be under most pressure at present from rate hikes and the tax hike on investors.



“So I suspect on its own the tougher regulations would only have a very minor impact, but coming at a time when there is already downward pressure on property prices, they may have the impact of magnifying the weakness particularly for upper end property and suburbs,” he said. Nicola Powell, Domain’s chief economist, says new anti-money laundering laws are not having a significant impact on property prices. Renee Nowytarger Reports from Canada, which also had a flood of criminal money funnelled through its Pacific Rim property hot spots like Vancouver, also equivocated on the potential impact. While an earlier study from 2019 found that criminal money may have raised prices in British Columbia by 5 per cent, a 2022 Cullen Commission report found that money laundering is not a significant cause of housing affordability issues or rising real estate prices. “While the impact of money laundering and anti-money laundering measures on real estate prices is something that would benefit from further study, I am unable to conclude that money laundering is a significant cause of housing affordability in the residential real estate market,” Cullen concluded.
